SERMON ON THE NATIVITY OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST.

By God's favour, dearly beloved brothers, the day is now near on which we long to celebrate with joy the birth of the Lord our Saviour. So I ask and urge you: let us strive as far as we can, with God's help, so that on that day we may approach the Lord's altar with a sincere and pure conscience, a clean heart and a chaste body, and may be worthy to receive his body and blood not for judgement but as a remedy for our souls. For our life rests in the body of Christ, as the Lord himself said: "Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will have no life in you." Let anyone who wants to receive life, then, change his life. For if he does not change his life, he will receive life to his judgement, and will be corrupted by it rather than healed, killed rather than brought to life. For so the apostle said: "Whoever eats the body of the Lord and drinks his blood unworthily eats and drinks judgement upon himself." And although it is fitting for us at all times to be adorned and resplendent with good works, it is especially so on the day of the Lord's birth, as the Lord himself said in the gospel: "Your works ought to shine before all people."

Consider, brothers, I beg you: when some powerful or noble man wishes to celebrate his own birthday or his son's, with what zeal, many days beforehand, he orders that whatever he sees dirty in his house be cleaned and made fine, whatever is unsuitable and out of place be thrown out, and whatever is useful and needed be provided. The house too, if it is dingy, is whitewashed; the floors are swept with brooms and adorned with a scattering of various flowers; and whatever contributes to the joy of the soul and the pleasures of the body is provided with every care. Why does he do all this, dearest brothers, except so that his birthday may be celebrated with joy? You who are going to die, if you prepare so much for your own birthday or your son's, how much, and what kind of things, ought you to prepare when you are about to welcome the birthday of your Lord? If you prepare such things for one who will die, what ought you to prepare for one who is eternal? Whatever, then, you would not want to find in your house, labour as far as you can that God may not find it in your soul. Surely, if an earthly king or any head of a household invited you to his birthday, with what clothing you would take care to go adorned — how new, how bright, how splendid — so that no oldness, no shabbiness or filth in them might offend the eyes of the one who invited you!

With the same zeal, then, strive as far as you are able, with Christ's help, so that your soul, arrayed with the various ornaments of the virtues and adorned with the jewels of simplicity and the flowers of sobriety, may go forth to the feast of the eternal King, that is, the birth of the Lord our Saviour, with a pure conscience: shining with chastity, resplendent with charity, gleaming white with almsgiving. For if Christ the Lord sees that you are so arrayed to celebrate his birthday, he will deign to come in person and not only to visit your soul but also to rest and dwell in it forever, as it is written: "I will walk among them and dwell in them"; and again: "Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone rises and opens to me, I will come in to him and dine with him, and he with me." How happy is the soul that, with God's help, has so taken care to govern its life that it is worthy to receive Christ as its guest and its dweller! And on the contrary, how unhappy is that conscience, to be mourned with a whole fountain of tears, which has so bloodied itself with evil deeds, darkened itself with the blackness of avarice, burned itself in the fire of anger, defiled itself with constant lust, and ruined itself under the tyranny of pride, that it is not Christ who begins to rest in it but the devil who begins to rule it. Such a soul, unless the medicine of penance quickly comes to its aid, will be abandoned by the light and seized by darkness; it will be emptied of sweetness and filled with bitterness; it will be invaded by death and rejected by life. Yet let a soul that is in this state not lose confidence in the Lord's mercy, nor be broken by excessive despair; rather, let it run back quickly to penance and, while the wounds of its sins are still fresh and warm, apply healing remedies to them. For our physician is almighty, and he is accustomed to heal our wounds in such a way that he does not even leave the traces of scars behind.

And therefore, dearly beloved brothers, just as at all times you must abstain from adulteresses and wretched concubines, so also you must abstain from your own wives for many days beforehand whenever you intend to celebrate either the Lord's birth or the other feasts. Above all, flee drunkenness; fight against anger as against a most savage beast; drive hatred out of your hearts like a deadly poison; and let there be such charity in you that it reaches not only to your friends but even to your enemies themselves, so that you may say with confidence in the Lord's Prayer: "Forgive us our debts," and the rest. For whoever knows that he hates even one person — I do not know whether he can approach the Lord's altar with confidence, especially since blessed John the evangelist cries out terrifyingly and says: "Whoever hates his brother is a murderer." It is now for you to judge whether a murderer, before he does penance, ought to presume to receive the Eucharist. Saint John adds still more and cries out, saying: "Whoever hates his brother is in darkness and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes"; and again he says: "Everyone who does not love his brother will remain in death"; and again: "If anyone says of himself that he loves God, and hates his brother, he is a liar. For whoever does not love his brother, whom he sees, how can he love God, whom he does not see?" Whoever, then, keeps hatred or anger in his heart and is neither frightened nor roused by such thunder must be considered not asleep but dead.

Reflecting constantly on these things, then, dearly beloved brothers, let those who are good strive with God's grace to persevere in good works, because it is not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered in the love of God to the end, who will be saved. But let those who recognize that they are slow to give alms, quick to anger and headlong in indulging lust hasten, with the Lord's help, to rescue themselves from evil, so that they may be worthy to do what is good; so that, when the day of judgement comes, they may not be punished with the ungodly and sinners, but may be worthy to attain the eternal rewards with the just and the merciful, by the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.
II. SERMON ON THE NATIVITY.

We read and faithfully hold that at the very beginning of the world's birth God made us, in the first man, in his own image and likeness. See: on this day, the roles reversed, God has been made in our likeness. In the first case he bestowed on us something better from what was his; in the second he took on something lower from what was ours. Through tasting the forbidden tree, the careless frailty of the first man tried, with damnable ambition, to grasp at the divinity of his Lord, at the persuasion of the devil, who said: "If you taste of this tree, your eyes will be opened and you will be like gods." Let us therefore recognize the wonderful goodness of our loving Father. Man, at the enemy's prompting, wished to become God through pride; and God became man through mercy. In a certain way the appearance of that ancient, newly begun age is renewed in us today through the divinity of Christ, when the first Adam was fashioned from the stuff of clay. See: now too the second Adam is formed in virgin flesh, as if from untouched and untilled earth. See, I say: once again, with the laws of nature suspended, a new man is brought to completion for a new life by the working of God alone. A virgin's son is promised, then, through the visitation of the Holy Spirit. What wonder is it if he is born without corruption who is conceived by sanctification? For it was not fitting that he who brought salvation to all of us should fail to grant to his mother alone the dignity of her integrity. "The Holy Spirit," it says, "will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you." It was plainly fitting that the mother who was to be honoured by a royal birth should first be sanctified by the entrance of the heavenly King. So let us not believe that our Lord and Saviour was a mere man just because we see that he was born as a man. It is not right that he should be believed not to be God, for whom, as he was about to descend to earth, a dwelling was prepared by God. And so, by the working of divine power, the womb of a believing woman is made fruitful; the tree of life is grafted onto mortal wood; the Power that carries all things is carried by weakness; and he who is not contained by earth, sea and sky is received within the limbs of a single little body. The Creator of all is born of his own creature; the great fountain springs from its own stream; the root of all things is born of its own shoot; and the true vine becomes the fruit of its own branch.

See, the most longed-for day is here, shining with a twofold grace: lit indeed with the brightness of its usual light, but gleaming above all with the splendour of a radiant womb. First of all, then, let us confess one God, our Lord, and there will be no second left whom we could call lesser. For whoever speaks of one as greater and another as lesser must admit that he holds two gods. Let us believe, therefore, in one God, Father and Son and Holy Spirit: three persons, not three substances; three names, and not three kingdoms. Why one God? Because there is one working of power, the same harmony of will, one divinity, one eternity, one majesty. And why three persons? Because the Father is one, the Son another, the Holy Spirit another; yet in the equality of divinity there is nothing different. For in the three there is one glory, one substance; equality of power makes the unity, while the distinctness of the names and the number of the persons make the Trinity. Let us therefore faithfully hold that our Lord Jesus Christ came into this world to save sinners: as wholly God from God, so wholly man from man, without the contagion of sin; equal to the Father according to his divinity, and according to his humanity lower even than the angels and younger than the mother whom he created.

These are the most solid foundations of our life and hope. It remains for the structure of good works to rise upon them for us, and this we shall certainly achieve by imitating him who became man from God precisely so that we might be able to imitate him. And we shall imitate God by disregarding the world, by not pursuing injuries done to us, by rejecting our own wills, by loving the glory of submission, by bearing tribulations with greatness of soul, by turning away from honours and riches and the pleasures of this body. So let us reserve all our delights there, all our rest for that homeland to come; let us crowd out the liberties and the allurements and desires of the present with longing for the things to come, sighing for that place every day, keeping before our hearts at every moment what eye has not seen nor ear heard, thinking without ceasing how we may worthily go to meet him at the second coming of his awesome majesty, when we must give an account of our deeds, our words and our thoughts; so acting, and so persevering in our place [?], as though we were to pass from this life every day. O day, the newness of all days, the gain of light and the loss of blindness, on which the eternal Sun, descending from the highest height of the Father's brightness, opened the entrance of a virgin's womb and spread its brilliant radiance over the gloom of the whole world! Lead the festal rejoicing, you faithful of Christ! A new thing has been done for us today, one that was long ago promised: that a mother's breasts should nurse a son without any loss to the virgin's chastity.

This is that newness announced by the prophecy of Jeremiah: "The Lord," he says, "will do a new thing upon the earth"; and, as if lighting a lamp in this obscurity, he at once added: "A woman will encompass a man." This, I say, is the new thing which I say the Lord will do upon the earth: that a woman will encompass a man. Pay attention, brothers, and better still, let your understanding run ahead of me. "A woman," he says, "will encompass a man." O woman blessed above women, who both did not know a man and encompassed a man in her womb; who is not touched by carnal union, and yet rejoices in offspring of flesh from a spiritual seed! Mary encompasses a man by giving faith to an angel, because Eve lost a man by consenting to a serpent. "The Lord," he says, "will do a new thing upon the earth." So when the time came for this newness to be shown, a heavenly messenger was sent ahead to the virgin; the angel greeted a girl who knew nothing of a man's greeting. The virgin is frightened by the strangeness of the words, and the angel says to her: "Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favour with the Lord." Do not be frightened, he means, at the sight of me, mother of my Lord; I have come as the minister of your conception. He himself sent me to you who is to be born of you; he himself announces joy to you through me, he who has been pleased to join the human nature to himself in a mystical marriage in your womb. "You have found favour with God; behold, you will conceive and bear a son" — not a man of ordinary merit, but the Saviour of the whole world. Do not be afraid, he says; cast all fear away from you, you who are to conceive the joy of the world. Turn over, Mary, the prophetic reading. For knowledge of the divine books cannot have passed you by, you who are to give birth to the very fulfilment of the prophets. Recall the virgin you have read of in the book of the prophet Isaiah, and rejoice, because you are she: you have been found worthy to be her. You were foreshadowed there as the virgin. Behold, you will conceive in your womb not by a man but by the Holy Spirit; you will be with child and remain undefiled; you will bear a son and suffer no loss of your virginity. And she said: "Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word." Then, as soon as the virgin's consent had been received, the angel returned to the dwellers of the heavenly realm, and behold, suddenly an ineffable power entered the virgin's secret place. The Maker of the world enters the narrow confines of a human womb; the untouched mother becomes pregnant; and behold, like a bridegroom from his chamber, Christ comes forth from Mary's womb. The power of majesty is hidden in the limbs of an infant; God hangs at the breast, is covered with the squalor of cheap swaddling cloths, endures the cramped hardness of a manger, and in his mercy humbly suffers it all, so that the world, which had perished, might be set free.

O blessed infancy, through which the life of our race was restored! O most welcome and delightful wailings, through which we escaped the gnashing of teeth and eternal weeping! O happy swaddling cloths, with which we wiped away the filth of our sins! O splendid manger, in which there lay not the hay of animals, but in which the food of angels was found! Nurse, Mary, your Creator; nurse the bread of heaven; nurse the ransom of the world. Offer the breast to him as he suckles, so that he himself may offer his cheek for you to the one who strikes him. Let the infant be nourished with the milk of your breasts, so that as a young man he may take a drink of vinegar for you. Let your hands carry him now, so that his arms may later be nailed to the cross for you. Finally, as his mother, supply him with sustenance in time, so that he, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, may grant eternal life to us and to you. Amen.
III. SERMON ON THE FEAST OF SAINT STEPHEN.

The reading from the Acts of the Apostles that was read to us today, dearly beloved brothers, holds a great deal to wonder at on its surface, yet it holds no less of dignity in its hidden meaning. "Look," says blessed Stephen, "I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God." Consider more carefully, dearly beloved brothers: when the blessed martyr had seen our Lord Jesus Christ standing at the right hand of God the Father, why did he declare that he saw the Son of Man and not rather the Son of God? Surely he would have seemed to pay the Lord greater honour if he had said that he saw the Son of God rather than the Son of Man. But there was a definite reason why it had to be shown this way in heaven and proclaimed this way in the world. The whole stumbling block of the Jews lay in this: that our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to the flesh was the Son of Man, should be said to be the Son of God as well. That is why divine Scripture so fittingly records that the Son of Man stood at the right hand of God the Father: so that, to confound the unbelief of the Jews, he whom the faithless denied in the world was shown to the martyr in heaven, and heavenly truth bore witness to him whom earthly impiety refused to believe. Hence, although, as the psalm that was read says, the death of his saints is precious in the sight of the Lord, still, if there can be any difference among martyrs, the one who came first would seem to stand out above all the rest. For although holy Stephen was ordained a deacon by the apostles, he went ahead of the apostles themselves by a blessed and triumphant death. So he who was lower in rank became first in suffering, and he who was a disciple in standing became a master by his martyrdom, fulfilling what the blessed prophet said in the psalm that was read: "What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?" For Stephen the martyr wished to be the first to render to the Lord what he had received from the Lord together with the whole human race. The death that the Saviour deigned to suffer for all, he was the first to pay back to the Saviour.

After this, sacred Scripture adds: "Kneeling down, he cried out, saying, 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them.'" See, dearly beloved brothers, the heart of this blessed man; see his great and wonderful love. He was in the midst of persecution, and he was praying to the Lord for his persecutors; and under a shower of stones, when another man could have forgotten even those dearest to him, he was commending his enemies to the Lord. For what did he say as he was being stoned? "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." At that moment he grieved more over their sins than over his own wounds, more over their wickedness than over his own death. And rightly more. In their wickedness there was much that ought to be lamented, but in his death there was nothing that ought to be grieved. Eternal death followed their wickedness, but everlasting life followed his death. Let us then imitate in some measure, dearly beloved brothers, the faith of so great a master and the love of so glorious a martyr. Let us love our brothers in the Church with the same spirit with which he then loved his enemies. But what is worse, sometimes we not only fail to love our enemies, we do not even keep faith wholly with our friends. Yet someone says, "I cannot love my enemy, whom I suffer every day like a most cruel foe." O whoever you are, you pay attention to what a man has done to you, and you do not consider what you have done to God. Since you have committed far graver sins against God, why will you not forgive a man a small thing, so that God may deign to forgive you everything?

Call to mind what Truth itself promised you in the Gospel, what guarantee, so to speak, it gave you, what kind of agreement it made with you: "If you forgive men their sins," it says, "your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offences. But if you do not forgive men, neither will your Father forgive you your debts." You see, brothers, that, with God's grace, how we are to be judged by the Lord has been placed in our own power. "If you forgive," he says, "you will be forgiven." I have said it often already, brothers, and I ought to say it more often still: let no one deceive himself, let no one lead himself astray, for whoever holds even one person in this world in hatred will lose everything he has offered to God in good works, because it is written: "Whoever hates his brother is a murderer." Here by "brother" we must understand every human being, for we are all brothers in Christ. So let no one without love presume upon his virginity, let no one trust in his almsgiving, his fasting or his prayers; for as long as he holds enmity in his heart, he will not be able to win God's favour by these or by any other good works. But if he wants to have God gracious to him, let him not disdain to hear good counsel. Let him listen not to me but to his Lord himself: "If you are offering your gift at the altar," he says, "and there you remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go first to be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift." Yet we, with quarrels within us and schemes turning over in our hearts, presume to approach the altar as though we had a good conscience, not fearing what is written: "Whoever eats the body of the Lord and drinks his blood unworthily eats and drinks judgement upon himself."

But someone says, "It is a great labour to love an enemy and to pray for persecutors." We do not deny it, brothers. It is indeed no small labour in this world, but the reward in the world to come is great. For by loving a human enemy you become a friend of God, indeed not only a friend but also a son, as he himself said: "Love your enemies," and so on. If some powerful and rich man in this world wanted to adopt you as his son, how you would serve him! What indignities, even from his slaves, what harsh and sometimes even shameful services you would endure, in order to come into his perishable and fragile inheritance! What another endures for earthly wealth, then, you endure for eternal life. For we are convicted by the surest reasoning that we are able to bear injury for God's sake, but we are unwilling. Indeed, if some powerful person does us an injury, even if he insults us to our face, we do not dare to answer with any harsh word, let alone pay him back. Why is that? So that we may not suffer still worse things from that powerful person than we have already borne. What the fear of man wrings from us, the love of Christ ought to demand of us. So if a powerful person rages against us, we keep silent and dare say nothing; but if an equal, or perhaps an inferior, offers us even a slight insult, we rise up like a wild beast, without any patience and without any thought of God, and either avenge our injury on the spot or at least prepare our minds to pay it back with something worse. What is this, that when a powerful person has injured us we take it patiently, but when an inferior has done so we are inflamed with excessive fury? It is because where we have feared man, we refuse to fear God here.

Therefore I ask you, brothers, that as far as we can, with God's help, we prepare our hearts for patience, and that in all things, and toward wicked people, we strive to act as physicians, hating not the people themselves but their wickedness. Let us pray for the good, that they may always climb to better things; for the wicked, that they may quickly take refuge in amendment of life and in the remedies of repentance. May he deign to grant this at our prayers, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God for ever and ever. Amen.
4. A SERMON ON SAINT STEPHEN.

Whenever we have to urge you, beloved, according to the Lord's command, to love your enemies, I fear that some may think and say that they cannot possibly fulfil it. Perhaps they also want to object that they cannot always imitate Christ. Look, I am speaking to you, O man, whoever you are who say that you cannot imitate your Lord in loving your enemies. Surely blessed Stephen was a man and not God; he was what you are, and what he did, he did only by the gift of the one you too pray to. Yet see what he did. He was speaking to the Jews; he was severe, and he loved. I must show you both, both the severe man and the loving one. Hear him being severe. These are Stephen's words when he addressed the Jews: "You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you have always resisted the Holy Spirit. Which of the prophets did your fathers not kill?" You have heard him being severe. I must show you the other side; hear him loving as well. They became angry, burning more fiercely still, and repaying evil for good they ran for stones and began to stone the servant of God. Here, holy Stephen, I put your love to the test; here let us see you, here let us watch you, here let us behold you as conqueror of the devil and victor over him. See, blessed Stephen looks upon the one who hung for him and was nailed to the wood of the cross; that one was crucified, this one was stoned. That one said, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing." You, blessed Stephen, what do you say? Let me hear you and see you, so that perhaps I may be able to imitate you. First blessed Stephen, standing, prayed for himself and said, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." When he had said this, he bent his knees, and on bended knee he said, "Lord Jesus, do not hold this sin against them," and having said this, he fell asleep. O happy sleep and true rest! See what it is to rest blessedly: to pray for one's enemies.

But I ask you, Stephen, kindly explain to me what this meant: that you prayed for yourself standing and knelt for your enemies. If you were here with us, you would no doubt answer: "I prayed for myself standing because for myself, who had served God rightly, I did not have to labour in praying and obtaining; for whoever prays for a just man does not labour." That is why he prayed for himself standing. Then he came to pray for the Jews, for the killers of Christ, for the killers of the saints, for those who were stoning him. Because he saw that their wickedness was so great and excessive that it could hardly be pardoned, he knelt down.

Let us then imitate blessed Stephen, dearly beloved brothers, at least as far as God grants us; let us love not only our friends but also our enemies, for there is nothing by which we can so well redeem our sins, conquer the devil and please God. Indeed, the Lord himself said: "Give, and it will be given to you; forgive, and you will be forgiven"; and again: "If you forgive men their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offences," and so on. See, brothers, the mercy of our Lord. He has placed in our power how we shall be judged on the day of judgement. If we forgive, we shall be forgiven; if we do not forgive, we shall not be forgiven. Let us love, then, dearly beloved brothers, not only our friends but also our enemies, so that we may come before the tribunal of the eternal Judge with a clear conscience, saying: "Give, Lord, because we have given; forgive, because we have forgiven. We have done what you commanded; now fulfil what you promised." May he grant this, who lives with the Father and reigns with the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.
5. A SERMON ON THE FEAST OF THE HOLY INNOCENTS.

Today, dearest brothers, we celebrate the feast of those infants whom, as the text of the Gospel tells, King Herod put to death. Let our land, then, rejoice with the greatest exultation, the fruitful mother of heavenly soldiers and of such great powers. See, the unholy enemy could never have done the blessed little ones as much good by kindness as he did by hatred. For as the most sacred feast of this day makes plain, as much as wickedness abounded against the blessed little ones, so much did the grace of blessing shine forth in them. For we heard a little while ago that when King Herod was persecuting Christ, thousands of blessed boys were slain, as the prophet says: "Rachel weeping for her children, and she would not be consoled, because they are no more." O blessed mother of triumphant ones, homeland of illustrious warriors, rich in so many children! Though for a moment, to the eyes of onlookers, she seemed to be bereaved, she never needs consolation, nor does she weep for her children, for in losing them she gained them, so that her mourning might be stilled. Blessed are you, O Bethlehem in the land of Judah, who suffered the savagery of King Herod in the slaughter of the boys, who were found worthy to offer to God at a single stroke a white-robed people of defenceless infants.

It is fitting, then, that we celebrate the birthday of those whom the world brought forth more blessed for eternal life than the womb of their mothers brought forth, since they attained the dignity of everlasting life before they had the use of this present one. The precious death of other martyrs earned praise in their confession; the death of these found favour in its very completion, because at the very outset of a life just begun, the death that put an end to the present life gave them the beginning of glory. Herod's impiety tore them from their mothers' breasts while they were still nursing. They are rightly called the flowers of the martyrs: springing up in the midst of the cold of unbelief, they were the first buds of the Church to break forth, and a kind of frost of persecution withered them. Therefore it is fitting to pay the infants slain for Christ the rites of honour, not of grief, to offer vows at the sacraments, not tears, for the one who was the cause of their punishment was also the cause of their crown; the one who was the cause of hatred was also the cause of their reward. While Herod was preparing death for the little ones, Joseph was warned by an angel to take Christ the Lord into Egypt. Egypt was full of idols; now, after the persecution by the Jews and the assent of an unholy people to the killing of Christ, Christ deigns to pass over to nations given over to idols, and leaving Judea he is brought to an ignorant world to be worshipped.

And since we know from the divine Scriptures that good and just men have always suffered persecution from the wicked, if we consider carefully, we find that those who inflict it suffer greater torments than those who seem to suffer it. For every person who persecutes another in the body is known first to suffer persecution himself in his heart. Even if he takes something of his victim's property, he does himself greater harm, because no one has an unjust gain without a just loss. Where there is gain, there is loss: gain in the strongbox, loss in the heart. He took a garment and loses his faith; he acquires money and loses justice. But people do this because they refuse to give thought to the last day. If they were willing to think constantly about the day of their death, they would keep their minds from all greed and malice. But what they refuse to think about now for their own good, they will have to endure later without any remedy. For the last day will come to them, the day of judgement will come, when they will neither be allowed to increase their money nor be able to redeem themselves from eternal death by good works; for the sinner is struck with this punishment too, that in dying he forgets himself, who while he lived forgot God. The day of judgement will come, when the foundations of the mountains will be shaken and the earth will burn down to the lowest depths, when the heavens will be set ablaze and dissolved, when the sun will be darkened and the moon will not give its light and the stars will fall from heaven, when sinners and the ungodly will be cast into the furnace of fire and the smoke of their torments will rise for ever and ever. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. So a time will come, dearest brothers, when it will be ill with no one who is good and well with no one who is evil. The last day will come, I say, when the godly will be separated from the ungodly, the just from the unjust, those who praise God from those who blaspheme God; they will be separated so that, as has been said, it may be ill with no one who is good and well with no one who is evil.

Why then is it not so now? Perhaps it is so even now; but what is now hidden will then be made manifest. Read the divine Scripture; enter with me, if you can, into the sanctuary of God. Perhaps there, if I am able, I shall teach you. Or rather, learn with me from the one who taught me that even now it is not well with the wicked, and that it is better with the good than with the wicked, although the full happiness of the good has not yet come, nor has the final punishment of the wicked. If you pay careful attention to the law of God, perhaps you will understand with me that it is not well with the wicked. For I ask you and inquire of you: why is it ill with you? You will answer me: "Poverty pinches me, hardship presses on me, perhaps pain in my limbs, fear of an enemy." So it is ill with you because you suffer evils, and it is well with him who suffers his own evil self? There is a great difference between suffering evil and being evil; but you are not what you suffer. You suffer evil, and you are not evil. He does not suffer evil, and he is evil. Do not be deceived, then. It cannot be that it is ill with you, who suffer evil, and well with him, who is evil. Since he is evil, do you think he suffers no evil, when he suffers himself? Is it ill with you because you suffer another's evil in your body, and well with him who suffers his own evil self in his body? Is it ill with you, who perhaps have a bad life, and well with him who has a bad soul? You who have good things, be good. Riches are good, gold is good, silver is good too, good are households, good are possessions. All these are good, but as means for you to do good. Have the goods that make you good, [not those] that make you evil [?]. "What are these?" you say. Do judgement and justice. The things you have are good; be good yourself among your goods. Let your goods put you to shame; do not be evil among them, lest you perish with them. God, the creator and governor of all things, has distributed gold and silver among people in such a way that it is good in itself by its nature and kind, yet its abundance does not puff up the good, nor does its lack crush them. But the wicked it blinds when it is offered them and torments when it is taken away, because when money is acquired it gives a false joy, and when it is lost it leaves behind a real sorrow.

Let us learn, then, to love true riches, that is, chastity, justice, peace and mercy. These riches are called just because they are granted to the good and the just for their merits; they are called true riches because whoever has them will not be in want, since, as the Apostle says, having food and clothing he is content with these. It is wrong, then, to think these earthly riches are riches, since they do not take away want. For the more greedily a person loves them and the more of them he has, the more he will burn with want. How then can they be riches, when as they grow, need grows; when the greater they are, the less they satisfy their lovers and the more they inflame their desire? Do you think that man rich who would be in less need if he had less? Hence someone put it well: "The love of money grows as much as the money itself grows." With the increase of money, the madness of greed increases. For all the avaricious and the covetous seem to be sick with a kind of dropsy. Just as a man with dropsy thirsts more the more he drinks, so the avaricious or covetous man is endangered by acquiring and is never satisfied by seeking.

But we, brothers, bearing in mind that we are pilgrims and guests in this world, should keep for ourselves on the journey of this life only what is needed for food and clothing, and as far as we can, send the rest ahead into eternal blessedness through alms to the poor, so that when on the day of judgement the covetous and avaricious, for their barrenness in good works, deserve to hear, "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire," we, for our good works, may hear, "Come, you blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world; for I was hungry and you gave me food to eat, I was naked and you clothed me." May the Lord bring us under his protection to that blessedness, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.
6. A SERMON ON THE FEAST OF THE APOSTLES JAMES AND JOHN.

I ask you, dearest brothers, not to take it amiss or think us tiresome for urging you so often to love your enemies. We do this because we know that no medicine is stronger for healing the wounds of all sins. And do not think it out of place that sometimes, even on the feasts of the martyrs, we call you to the love of enemies. We wish to do this because we know that all the martyrs reached the crown of martyrdom through this most perfect love, and we rejoice with great wonder that this was fulfilled in blessed Stephen too. Listen carefully, I beg you, brothers, and understand that in all wicked people it is their vices we ought to hate, not the people themselves: love the person, hate the vice. Do not love the vice for the sake of the person, and do not hate the person for the sake of the vice. The person is your neighbour; the vice is your neighbour's enemy. You truly love your friend when you hate the vice that harms your friend. If you believe this, you do well, for the righteous live by faith. I am speaking of something that is all too common in human affairs. Sometimes someone becomes the enemy of your dearest friend, someone who used to be the friend of you both. Of three friends, two begin to be enemies of each other. What is the one left in the middle to do? One of those who hate each other wants you to hate along with him the one he hates, and says to you: "You are no friend of mine, because you are a friend of my enemy." And what this one says to you about that one, that one says to you about this one. There were three of you; two have fallen out, and you alone are left. If you join this one, you will hate the other as an enemy; if you join that one, you will hate this one; if you side with both, both will grumble. There is the temptation. Perhaps you are waiting to hear from me what you should do. Remain the friend of both. Let those who are at odds with each other be reconciled through you. If you have heard anything bad said by one about the other, do not betray it to the other, lest those who are now enemies later become friends again and betray their betrayers to each other.

But I have said this with regard to human beings, not with regard to the eyes of God. See, no one betrays you to God. It is God who sees you, God who judges you. You heard a word from someone angry, someone hurt and inflamed: let it stay with you. Why should it be betrayed, why should it be brought out? It will not burst you if it stays inside you. Indeed, speak to the friend who wants to make you the enemy of your friend; address him, and treat his soul, as one sick, with the gentleness of medicine. Say to him: "Why do you want me to be his enemy?" He will answer: "Because he is my enemy." "So you want me to be the enemy of your enemy? I ought to be the enemy of your sin. The one you want to make me an enemy of is a human being; you have another enemy, and it is to him that I ought to be an enemy if I am your friend." He will answer: "Who is this other enemy of mine?" "Your vice." He will answer: "What is my vice?" "The hatred with which you hate your friend."

Be like a doctor, then. A doctor does not love the sick person unless he hates the sickness. To free the patient, he attacks the fever. Do not love your friends' vices, if you love your friends. But to whom am I saying this—do you suppose I do not do it myself? What I say, my brothers, I do, if I do it in myself. And I do it first in myself if I receive from the Lord a hatred of my own vices, offer my heart to the physician to be healed, attack my sins as far as I can, groan over them, confess that they are in me, and accuse myself. You who were reproaching me, correct yourself. This is justice, so that it may not be said to us: "You see the speck in your brother's eye, and do not see the beam in your own eye. Hypocrite, first take the beam out of your own eye." Anger is a speck, hatred a beam; but you nourished the speck, and it becomes a beam. Anger grown old becomes hatred; a speck nourished becomes a beam. So that the speck may not become a beam, do not let the sun go down on your anger. Do you see and feel yourself livid with hatred, and yet reproach someone who is angry? Remove hatred from yourself, and then you rightly reproach anger. There is a speck in his eye; in yours there is a beam. And how can an eye with a beam in it see a speck? I do not know with what face someone who harbours hatred in his heart reproaches a person who is angry for a moment [?]. One who is angry for a moment, quickly angered and quickly appeased, does indeed incur a speck, but at once removes it through repentance. But whoever keeps hatred in his heart for a long time, by nourishing the speck, turns it into a beam. There is a beam in your eye because you would not at once remove the speck that sprang up there. You slept with it, you rose with it, you cultivated it within yourself, you watered it with false suspicions, you nourished it by believing the words of flatterers and of those who brought you evil reports about your friend; you did not pull the speck out by your own diligence, and you made a beam.

Take the beam out of your eye: do not hate. Do you fear your brother or not? I tell you, do not hate, and you are safe. You reply and say to me: "What is hating, and what harm is there in a person hating his enemy?" You hate your brother, yet you make light of hatred. Hear the divine Scripture: "Whoever hates his brother is a murderer." So if he is a murderer—though you prepared no poison, did not go out with a sword to strike your enemy, did not procure an accomplice for the crime, nor a place, nor a time, and in the end did not commit the crime itself—you merely hated, and you killed yourself before you killed him. Learn justice, then, so that you hate nothing but a person's vices. If you hold to this and practise this justice, preferring to heal even vicious people rather than condemn them, you will come happily before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, not to be condemned for hatred but to be crowned for love and peace, by the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.
VII. ON THE EPIPHANY

Recently, dearest brothers, we celebrated the sacrament of the day of our redemption, on which God clothed himself in humanity with its weaknesses. Today we honour the day on which God revealed himself in humanity by mighty works: on this day he either gave a star in the sky as herald of his birth, or turned water into wine at the wedding feast in Cana of Galilee, or consecrated the waters by his own baptism in the waves of the Jordan for the renewal of the human race, or fed five thousand people with five loaves. In each of these are contained the mysteries and the joys of our salvation. For he was born of the Virgin for us, as the star showed. By the miracle of his work and the changing of the water he signified that we are to be changed for the better; he provided remedies for us from baptism, which he offered in the bed of the Jordan and [?] called us to. And so, dearest brothers, in all our actions let us carry the star of faith before us, and let us celebrate the baptism of Christ as a safeguard of purity, for this rebirth of Christ is also the confirmation of your faith. He made known to you the benefit of his gift through the example of a second birth, and what he wanted you to do, he did first.

We read that the Jews had various baptisms under the Law, but none of them could provide a universal medicine against the evil of transgression. And so, for the absolution of the whole world, the waters of rebirth needed to be sanctified from heaven; and because the human race throughout the whole world needed the sacrament of baptism, he gave a blessing to all waters when, with unique and singular love, he went down into the bed of the Jordan. For then the water did not so much wash Christ the Lord as it was itself washed. For it was for you that Christ came by being born, for you that he fought by living, for you that he did battle by dying. The one you see dead for you, understand to have been baptized for you. Thus Christ the Lord was entirely the same before his baptism as he was after it. And so his forerunner and baptizer, when Christ came to him to be baptized, addressed him thus: "Lord, I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?" What could be clearer, what stronger, concerning the purity of Christ before he was baptized? "I ought to be baptized by you"—that is: you who are the fount of innocence and the fullness of righteousness, who, needing nothing, know how to give and do not know how to receive—"I ought," he says, "to be baptized by you, for you bring with you and possess in yourself the gifts of purity and the sacraments of baptism; and what I shall give by grace, through your bounty, you hold by nature." Meanwhile the creature gains. At the touch of the Creator his limbs are dipped and the streams are enriched. By life-giving grace the body is not changed by the river, but the river by the body. The blessed water marvels that its own source has come down into it; in a single moment it conceives eternal remedies and, made fruitful, gives birth to a generation to be renewed, giving back what it had received and receiving what it did not have.

In all this it would be astonishing that the Lord submitted himself to the blessing of a servant, had he not also submitted himself to the cross and to death. And by the worth of the very price he paid, he taught us thoroughly how precious humanity is to him. But from this we also understand how grave our Lord judges the case of human crimes to be, since on their account he sent to earth not an angel, not an archangel, but God. How grievous and how hard the state of sin is, the greatness of the remedy reveals. How severe the examination of evils will be by which they are condemned is shown by the care with which they are redeemed.

Let us therefore be on our guard with all vigilance and diligence, lest the devil wound what God has healed, lest by the consent of the heart or by the vice of the body we offer to the enemy the service that we owe rather to the Lord. If some violent and powerful man had seized something of our property and possessions, would we not think him deserving of the utmost hatred, and rightly loathe him as an enemy? With what mind, then, do we consent through sin to the devil, who seeks to take from us not our property but our life, to rob us not of land but of heaven, not to narrow the bounds of our estate but to deprive us of the boundless expanses of eternity? Amid all this, O man, if you will measure the dignity of your making and your Lord's love toward you by the price paid, you will be able to have no doubt about the kingdom.

As for what we heard just now when the gospel was read—that on the third day a wedding took place in Cana of Galilee and that water was turned into wine—let us see what that wedding is. Here our acquisition, or rather our restoration, is shown by the vows and festivities of a wedding, just as in another place the return of the younger son is greeted with dancing and music. The six jars are the six ages of this world: the first from Adam to Noah, from Noah to Abraham, from Abraham to David, from David to the exile in Babylon, from the exile in Babylon to John the Baptist. In these times prophecy concerning Christ was never lacking, and through these ages the righteous displayed a figure and type of the Lord. They hold two or three measures each, because they contain within them faith in the Trinity. But let us see what the divine word says. Let us treat the sacred oracles of the gospel themselves.

In Cana of Galilee he turned water into wine and by the power of his works disclosed the Lord hidden beneath the man. "And on the third day," it says, "there was a wedding." But what is this wedding but the joy of human salvation? Why on the third day? Either because it shows us the mystery of the Trinity, or because he rose on the third day. So, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, he came down to earth to be joined, by taking flesh, to the Church that was to be gathered from the Gentiles. To this Church, which is of course ourselves, he gave both a pledge and a dowry. He gave the pledge when he was promised to us by the Law; he gave the dowry when he was sacrificed for us. This can also be taken another way, so that we understand the pledge as present grace and the dowry as eternal life. Let us see what he does in Cana of Galilee. Here now let astonishing miracles reveal God to us.

Jars are set out holding two or three measures each. The jars are filled. Suddenly the waters are changed—waters that would later change human beings—and, being changed for the better, they speak, as it were, of the power of baptism. In a certain way the likeness of rebirth is expressed in them; and as one thing is made from another, as a lower creature is transformed into a more pleasing form, the mystery of the second birth is revealed. Nothing of the waters' quantity is diminished, and while remaining themselves they depart wholly from themselves by a noble transformation. They lose their own substance and acquire another's. A stronger flavour is gained by the thin matter, a hidden power is poured into the light streams, the nature of the waters becomes intoxicating, and so in a new manner they confess the power of their Creator. Who can transform these things except the one who was able to create them?

So when the wine ran short, his mother said to [?] him: "They have no wine." First let us ask what the wine was that is said to have run short, and what is the other wine that is wonderfully provided, which the steward of the feast declares to be better, saying: "Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then what is poorer. But you have kept the good wine until now." In many places we take wine to mean the divine commandments and the holy Scriptures, which contain the purest strength of heavenly wisdom, by which the senses are warmed to love of the Lord and the affections are intoxicated, according to what is said of Wisdom: "She has set her table; she has mixed her wine in the bowl." So when the power of the divine Scriptures has filled someone's inner being, he will be able to say with the prophet: "You have given us the wine of compunction to drink," and: "How glorious is your intoxicating cup!" So by Christ's working in Cana of Galilee the wine ran out and wine was made: that is, the shadow is removed and the truth presented, the Law withdraws and grace succeeds it, carnal things are exchanged for spiritual, the old observance is poured over into the New Testament, as the blessed Apostle says: "The old things have passed away; behold, in Christ all things have been made new." And just as those jars filled with water lose nothing of what they were and yet begin to be what they were not, so the Law did not perish when it was fulfilled by the coming of Christ, but advanced. So when the wine runs short, another wine is served. The Old Testament is indeed good, but without spiritual understanding it fades away in the letter, whereas the New has given back the fragrance of life in grace.

This being so, let us consider the steward himself, the one in charge in the bridegroom's house, and whom we can understand him to be. Whom else should we understand but blessed Paul, who, after receiving the Law, was filled and intoxicated with the sweetest fragrance or taste of the mysteries of the New Testament and the fragrance of spiritual senses, and cries out in praise: "You have kept the good wine until now." Yet let us see how he praises this wine: "Eye has not seen," he says, "nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him." Here are true miracles, here are miracles worth proclaiming, which are worked in us when he made the good out of the very wicked, the humble out of the proud, the chaste out of the shameless, friends of God out of followers of the world. What greater miracles can he perform than when he deigns to raise a human being—a worm and rottenness—to an angelic state, to set him among heavenly things instead of earthly ones, and to take him into the grace of his adoption? May he deign to grant this, who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever.
VIII. ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD, AT MASS, OR ON THE FEAST OF LUCIAN THE MARTYR

Dearest brothers, we have celebrated the feast of our Lord's nativity with the faith by which we believe that God was born of a human being. Let us therefore honour this feast with the devotion by which God was revealed in a human being. There he was hidden in weaknesses; here he is revealed in mighty works. For today a star, which was to show Christ to those seeking him, led the Magi coming from the east all the way to the place where the Saviour was born. Let the holy birth be beheld beneath a lowly hut. He who shines in the stars is adored in swaddling clothes. He is adored in swaddling clothes: that is, inviolate majesty beneath the abasement of human corruption. Through a hinted mystery the greatness of divine mercy is revealed in this, that Ethiopians—that is, Gentiles—are the first to come to Christ. The firstfruits of the nations are consecrated to the knowledge of the truth; the Church of the Gentiles, stripped of the blackness of sin and about to be clothed in the whiteness of faith, goes before the synagogue of the Jews. So she seeks our salvation in the manger. What does it mean that she seeks our salvation in the manger? It means that the multitude of unbelieving peoples, once wild, is received into the stable of the Church and grows tame. The Jews indeed boast that the worship of God belongs to them, but the first envoys of the Gentiles see Christ. Why first? Because the healthy eye of the Christian follows the light, whereas the diseased gaze of the Jews is clouded by the light itself, and their sick sight grows darker when light is brought to it.

Meanwhile the blessed embassy marvels that it has been led to the holy cradle by a ray running down from above. The most distant nation is the first to enjoy the common good. By what astonishing condescension is he who embraces earth and heaven enclosed in his mother's arms; he who surpasses his Father's kingdom lies hidden in his mother's lap. Through a simple act of service a spiritual secret is revealed: the humanity is seen, the divinity adored. They present gold, frankincense and myrrh, offering more in mystery than they themselves understood. In the gift of gold royal dignity is shown, in the smoke of the frankincense divine majesty, in the form of the myrrh a humanity destined for burial. And so the number of the gifts speaks of the Trinity, and the single act of devotion bears witness to the unity.

Therefore let us strive to look up to heaven with the ever-watchful attention of the heart, if we desire to come to Christ. May the star of righteousness direct for us the paths of a perfect life. To him who said, "You shall not appear before me empty-handed," let us offer the gold of faith, the spices of devotion, the burnt offerings of chastity. Let us have spiritual myrrh within us, which may so embalm our souls as to keep them unharmed by the corruption of sin. Let us change our road if we wish to reach our homeland—our heavenly homeland, that is. Let this be the exchange between the two: that by the use of this life we may acquire possession of that one, and that, just as eternal life will be the reward of this life, so we may labour that this life may be the merit that earns that one. As for what the evangelist says, that the Magi were warned in a dream not to return to Herod but to go back to their own country by another road, this is a spiritual command to us, that we should return to our homeland by another road, that is, by another way of life.

Perhaps someone asks how this can be done. Let whoever wishes to know this hear the prophet saying: "Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it." For in this way one returns to the homeland by another road. Since through pride we fell into the world, we must return to paradise through humility. Through greed we came into the devil's service; let us return to Christ the Lord through mercy. Through pleasure and self-indulgence we bore the devil's harshest yoke; let us hasten to take up Christ's light yoke through love and justice, so that we who, unhappily serving the devil along the roads of unbelief and wickedness, departed from the company of the angels, may strive to return to our original homeland along the roads of goodness and faith.

If in this way we are willing to leave the roads of death and keep to the roads of eternal life, then, transferred from the left hand to the right, we may faithfully and happily imitate the journey of the Magi. Does it not seem to you that someone is already returning to the homeland by another road who used to take other people's property and now longs to give away his own in mercy? Does it not seem to you that someone is walking by another road who was an adulterer and is now chaste, who was a drunkard and is now sober, who used to curse and now blesses, who was envious and is now kind? For if, with God's help, we strive by prayer together with good works to change the course of our lives for the better in this way, we shall be able to reach eternal blessedness, by the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.
IX. ON THE EPIPHANY

Yesterday, because of the labour of the vigils, we held back what we had to say about the feast. Now, if you wish, you can hear it at a more suitable time. A short while ago, dearly beloved brothers, we celebrated the birthday of the Lord our Saviour, on which he who comes before all ages and times and created them was born for us in time. Today, by the surest proofs, God has been made known in man: whether because he gave a star from heaven to announce his birth and made it go before the Magi who followed it, right up to the venerable cradle of the infancy he had taken on; or because in the bed of the Jordan he consecrated the waters by his baptism for all nations, for the salvation of the human race (for he, purer than all waters, entered them not to be sanctified but to sanctify); or because this is also the day of that miracle when, at a wedding feast in Cana of Galilee, he first turned water into wine. By that miracle he certainly shows that he would change all the nations, which like water were flowing away in the emptiest and most shallow thinking, to the true savour of spiritual wisdom and the pure truth of true faith. Whichever of these three it is, it holds the mysteries and the joys of our salvation. For either what the star showed was born for us of the Virgin, or what he consecrated in the bed of the Jordan was granted to us in baptism. And when he turned water into wine, he showed beforehand by the miracle he worked that we too were to be changed for the better.

And the Magi themselves, who came by the sign of the star to that venerable cradle of the heavenly child, what else did they express in those gifts but our faith? In that they offer three gifts, the Trinity is understood; and in that they are three and each offers one gift, unity in the Trinity is declared. By the gold a king is shown, by the frankincense God is recognized, and by the myrrh, which is used for embalming bodies, the burial of the man who was to be crucified is proclaimed. In keeping with this, beloved, let us too take on the role of the Magi in spiritual service. First of all, let us seek Christ for as long as it takes until we are found worthy to find him. Let the light of faith lead us like the star of heaven. Let it show him to us no longer crying in a manger but reigning in the highest citadel of heaven; to be worshipped not in his mother's lap but on his Father's throne; no longer to be judged in humility but coming in majesty to judgment. Let our offering of the three gifts be, as it were, a perfect confession of the Trinity. Let us believe in a unity joined without confusion and a Trinity distinguished without separation. Let the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be believed to be one God: three persons, and not three substances. As far as the order of the heavenly nature is concerned, one Godhead must be confessed in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit in such a way that neither is a single person supposed in the Trinity nor a threefold substance in the unity. Plurality is to be ascribed to the unity in such a way that equality is not taken away from the Trinity; and although number is admitted in the one Godhead, difference is not to be accepted. So the worship of God must be ordered in the hearts of the faithful in such a way that neither separation is admitted in the unity nor mixture in the Trinity.

For the day of the holy Nativity, dearly beloved brothers, is close to this day. Then the Lord was born, now he is baptized; then he begot us to life, now he has begotten us again to salvation. Then he took up lost Adam, now he washes the sinner clean. So he came to baptism, as it is written. But what was there for him to wash away, who was clean? Surely this: that he, being clean, might wash the unclean. The running waters were then poured over him, but they carried our sins away with them. The drops of baptism flowed down from him, but our crimes flowed away in those drops. O the mercy and the power of the Lord together! We were not yet in the world, and already we were being washed in baptism. We were cleansed by him before we were born. For this was the very purpose of baptism: that the waters which were to cleanse us should first be cleansed by him. And when he had come up out of the water, says Scripture, he saw the heavens opened. Had heaven only then been opened to him, whose eyes saw into the inner reaches of the heavens? No, heaven is opened so that the mystery of baptism might be declared in this: that when a person comes out of baptism, the gate of the heavenly kingdom is then opened to him. And what of this, that the Magi come to the newborn Lord, or rather are led to him? They see him laid in a manger, yet the lowliness of his birth does not lessen in their minds their reverence for his divinity. They worship him with their bodies, honour him with gifts, revere him with their service; with their eyes they see a man, and by their homage they confess God. For they saw that in him who had been born there was more for the minds of men to contemplate than for their eyes to see. The Lord, who had then been born in the body, through whom all things had been born, was seen in a manger but reigned in heaven; he was within a little body, yet he held all things within himself. He had indeed been born of a mother, but he himself had first created his mother. And so the Magi humbled themselves, because they saw the stars serving him; they recognized as God him whom the heavens served. For that reason their very gifts were full of divine mystery. For, as you have heard, they offered gold, frankincense and myrrh. So in the number of three gifts a threefold meaning is contained: in the frankincense they offered honour to God, in the gold royal dignity, in the myrrh the burial of the body.

So let us too, dearly beloved brothers, offer holy and sincere gifts to our God: faith, charity, patience, humble minds, upright conduct, souls worthy to have God dwell in them. These are the gifts pleasing to God, these the welcome offerings, which are indeed offered to him but profit those who offer them. For he needs nothing and no gift; the best gift to him is to have reasons for rewarding. He asks nothing more of us, seeks nothing more, than the salvation of our soul. For he counts everything as done for him by us if we so act that all things may be granted to us by him, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father for ever and ever. Amen.
X. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT FELIX.

To enlighten the human race, dearly beloved brothers, our Lord has kindled many spiritual lamps in this world, so that, as heavenly religion and teaching shine out through holy men, the darkness of error should never envelop anyone who wished to see the light of truth. And what are these lamps that our Lord has granted to dispel and illuminate the gloom of unbelief? First the patriarchs, then the prophets, after them the apostles, and finally all the priests of all the churches. Among them divine goodness granted to this city an outstanding and preeminent lamp, the lord Honoratus of holy memory, whom God saw fit to raise up on the lampstand of this church so that he might give light to all. Although he shone on this city with the special brilliance of his works, he nevertheless reached all places through the renown of his name and spread abroad the light of his merits. When we recall his unconquerable faith in his works, his wonderful firmness in despising the world, and his singular charity in mercy, we believe without doubt that he fulfilled martyrdom even without undergoing a martyr's death.

For martyrdom is not completed only by the shedding of blood, nor does the burning of flames alone bestow the palm. The crown is reached not only by the death of the body but also by contempt for it. Without wrong to the saints who died in the persecutions, let it be said: to have afflicted the flesh, overcome lust, resisted avarice, and triumphed over the world is a great part of martyrdom. And we, dearly beloved brothers, if we wish to attain to the fellowship [?] of the priests, let us think about imitating the martyrs. For they must recognize something of their own virtues in us if they are to see fit to pray to the Lord for us. If we cannot bear the torments the holy martyrs endured, let us at least, with their intercession, fight against evil desires. And since daily sins are never lacking, let daily remedies not be lacking either.

Let no one think he possesses any happiness or any true joy in this world. Blessedness can be prepared for here; it cannot be possessed here. Two times follow one another in their order: a time to weep and a time to laugh. Let no one deceive himself, brothers: in this world there is no time to laugh. I know, brothers, that everyone wants to rejoice, but they do not look for joy where it ought to be sought. True joy in this world never was, is not, and never can be. For this is how the Lord warned his disciples in the Gospel: "In this world you will have tribulation"; and again: "The world will rejoice, but you will be sorrowful; but your sorrow will be turned into joy." So in this life let us do what is good, with labour and pain and with the Lord's help, so that in the world to come we may gather the fruits of good works with joy and gladness, according to the saying: "Those who sow in tears will reap in joy."

In this world, then, dearly beloved brothers, we have been cast out of the blessed dwelling of paradise through the sin of the first man and sent as it were into exile; and so in this age we have no homeland, as the Apostle also says: "While we are in this body, we are exiles from the Lord." So let us not look for joy in this world, because, as was said above, true joy can be acquired here but not possessed here. Do not look on the road for what is being kept for you in the homeland. And since you must fight every day against the devil under Christ's leadership, do not look in the battle for the reward that is being kept for you in the kingdom. Do not look in the fight for what is being kept for you when the victory is complete. Pay attention rather to what the Apostle says: "All who want to live a godly life in Christ suffer persecution"; and again: "For through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God."

So, by God's gift, we must act in such a way that we may be found worthy to reach happily our principal homeland, where our fathers, the patriarchs, prophets and apostles, long to receive and see us; where also our fellow citizens, the angels, and that heavenly city Jerusalem, and Christ the king of that city wait for us with the arms of charity outstretched, so that, having overthrown the devil, we may hasten to them full of good works. For you know, brothers, that all merchants and all who are travelling are anxious on the road so that they may be secure in their homeland, and they have true gladness when they are found worthy to reach their homeland with great profit. So let us too, dearly beloved brothers, prepare our souls for joy at the time when we are found worthy to reach Christ. Meanwhile, let us rejoice now in hope, as those who will later have true joy in reality. What is worse, there are many who, in a perverse order, think they rejoice in the pleasures, delights and luxury of this world. But what they seem to sow in joy they will have to reap with tears and mourning, for he who said in the Gospel does not lie: "Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep." That is what that unhappy rich man did who was clothed in purple and fine linen. He had joy in the world, but he earned flames in hell. Lazarus, who lay at his gate, had sorrow on the road, but he received true joy in the homeland.

And we, dearly beloved brothers, let us beseech God's mercy as much as we can, that he may see fit so to breathe into us the love of eternal life that we would rather love the homeland than the road, and think more about the world to come than about the present one; and that we may always strive so to live in the exile of this world that we may come to the future judgment with a free and untroubled conscience, adorned with good works, by the grace of our Lord, to whom be honour and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
XI. AN ADMONITION ON THE DAY OF JUDGMENT.

I ask you, dearly beloved brothers, and with great humility I urge you, that none of you be angry with me or perhaps think me out of place or excessive because I strive so often to impress upon you the day of judgment, which we must tremble at and which it is profitable to dread. If there is anyone whom I perhaps displease in this, let him consider my danger and hear the Lord threatening the priest terribly through the prophet: "If you do not declare to the wicked man his wickedness, I will require his blood at your hand"; and again: "Cry out, do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their sins." But perhaps someone will say: "Why are such hard things constantly preached to us?" Because it is better to endure a little bitterness here and afterwards come to eternal sweetness than to have false joy here and endure punishment without end there. Listen, brothers, not to me but to the Lord saying in the Gospel: "Blessed are those who mourn now, for they will be comforted"; and: "Woe to you who laugh now, for you will weep and mourn." And consider this, brothers: whenever doctors of the body come to those who are sick in body, they cut out everything that seemed delightful to them and forbid entirely whatever is sweet. Sometimes they do not even allow them to take a cold drink; at times they make them drink the bitterest potions, and they often cut into their wounds with the harshest and sharpest instruments. What doctors of the body do for the health of bodies, then, spiritual doctors strive to do for the salvation of souls.

Thinking of this, dearly beloved brothers, and knowing well that I shall have to give an account before the tribunal of the eternal Judge both for my own salvation and for yours, I want to apply to you remedies which are harsh indeed but wholesome, so that afterwards I may be found worthy to rejoice with you in unending safety in the company of the angels. I do not suggest these things because I have sensed that you do not gladly receive our admonitions; but because I must preach more often both for your salvation and for mine, I am eager to rouse your minds both to fear the judgment and to long for the reward, so that, with the Lord's help, you may happily prepare the vats of your holy hearts to store the spiritual vintage, as you have always done. Whenever we preach something hard to you, we do not say it because we suspect you of doing such things; rather, we denounce even what you do not do so that we may heal the things in which you may perhaps have been caught. For it often happens that while greater evils are feared, lesser ones are more quickly avoided. Just as theriac is drunk so that poisons may not overpower the body, so stern preaching is applied to prepare antidotes for souls.

It is certain, dearly beloved brothers, that if we constantly think about the benefits of our God, which were conferred on us with no merits of ours going before, sins will either not master us or, if they have perhaps crept in, they will quickly be corrected by penance. For who could even conceive in his mind, let alone set out in words, how great are these benefits of our God toward us? He made us when we did not exist; he restored us afterwards when we had perished. He underwent death, he set us free with his precious blood, he descended into hell, he snatched us from the jaws of eternal death, he promised us the rewards of heaven. Thinking over all these things, dearly beloved brothers, with a devout and kindly mind, let us hasten, as far as we can and with his help, to repay his benefits. Let us not return evil for good, but, striving with all our strength to obey his will as far as we can, let us faithfully take care that his commandments bring us healing by our following them rather than judgment by our transgressing them.

For what shall we do, dearly beloved brothers, on that fearful day of judgment, when, as the world trembles and the trumpets of the angels sound before him, the Lord takes his seat on that throne of his majesty, surrounded by the light of the heavenly host; and there, with the human race raised from the bosom of the earth and the ancient dust, and with conscience standing as witness for each person, and with the punishments of sinners and the rewards of the just set in view, he begins to demand an account of their lives; and, now more just than merciful, with the severity of a judge he begins to accuse those guilty of despising his mercy, and to say: "O man, I made you from the clay with my own hands; I breathed spirit into earthly limbs; I saw fit to give you our image and likeness; I placed you amid the delights of paradise. You despised the life-giving commandments and preferred to follow the deceiver rather than the Lord. But I pass over the things of old. Afterwards, moved by mercy, when you had been driven out of paradise and were held in the chains of death by right of sin, I entered a virgin's womb, to be born without loss of her virginity. I lay exposed in a manger and wrapped in swaddling clothes; I bore the indignities of infancy and human sorrows, by which I became like you, for this purpose: to make you like me. I endured the slaps and spittle of those who mocked me; I drank vinegar mixed with gall. Beaten with scourges, crowned with thorns, fastened to the cross, pierced with a wound, I gave up my life amid torments so that you might be snatched from death. See the marks of the nails by which I hung fastened; see my side pierced with wounds. I took on your sorrows to give you my glory. I took on your death so that you might live for ever. I lay buried in the tomb so that you might reign in heaven. Why have you thrown away what I suffered for you? Why, ungrateful one, have you rejected the gifts of your redemption? I do not complain about my death. Give me back your life, for which I gave my own; give me back your life, which you have ceaselessly slain with the wounds of your sins. Why have you polluted with the filth of lust the dwelling I had consecrated for myself in you? Why have you stained with the foulness of allurements the body that was already mine? Why have you afflicted me with the cross of your crimes, heavier than the one on which I once hung? For the cross of your sins, on which I have hung against my will, is heavier to me than that cross which, taking pity on you, I mounted unwilling [?] in order to slay your death. Though I was immortal, for your sake I became a changeable man. Though I was incapable of suffering, for your sake I deigned to suffer. But you despised God in the man, salvation in the weak one, the way home in the way, pardon in the judge, life in the cross, healing in the punishments."

So, that we may escape this terrible rebuke, whenever any sins whatever creep up on us, let us hasten without any pretence to take refuge in the remedies of penance, so that, freed from the evil hearing, we may be found worthy to reach eternal forgiveness, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever.
XII. AN ADMONITION [?].

Just now, dearest brothers, as the divine reading was read, we heard the blessed apostle warning us in words both terrifying and salutary. For he says: "We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what is due for the things done in his body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil." The Lord too proclaims the same thing in the Gospel, saying: "The Son of Man will come in his glory with his angels, and then he will repay each one according to his works." Pay careful attention, I beg you, dearest brothers, and tremble together with me, for he did not say that he will repay each one according to his own mercy, but according to that person's works. Here he is merciful; there he is just. For his not punishing sinners at once is patience, not neglect. He has not lost his power; rather, he has kept us in reserve for repentance. So we must greatly fear that the longer he waits for us to be corrected, the more severely he will punish us if we refuse to amend.

Since this is so, dearest brothers, we ought to know and understand that nothing is more salutary for us than to condemn the pleasures of all present things and to think instead of when we shall pass from this world, or when, as the last day overtakes us, we shall lay aside the tent of our body and receive it back again at the time of the resurrection, so that together with it we may receive according to what we have done, whether good or evil. And so I ask you, brothers, that every day we think rather of what we shall be like on the day of judgment, when we are to be presented before the most pure gaze of the angels and must render an account to the eternal Judge from the books of conscience.
