For with all other proofs set aside, it is certain that on that day each person will be set before himself, his own soul will be shown to him in the mirror of his heart, and the witnesses against it will be brought forward not from somewhere outside but from within the soul itself. The testimony to be added will not be anything foreign but all too familiar, namely, its own works. The unhappy soul's sins and crimes will be ranged before it, so that the proof may convict it and the recognition put it to shame, according to what is written: "I will rebuke you and set it before your face." Whoever neglects to amend himself now, while he may, will first suffer the punishment of shame before that heavenly people; and the soul that now neglects to heal the rot of its sins by the short and easy settlement of repentance will remain wounded for ever, without any remedy, before that dreadful judgment seat.

Since this is so, it would go well with us if we now repented of our evils as we shall then repent without any remedy, if we could see and shudder at our foulness and our shame now, just as we shall see them then. Oh, if only it were possible even now to look upon the face of the sinful soul with the eyes of the body, and if we were permitted to bring the countenance of our conscience before our eyes! If that were possible, words cannot say with what zeal and what fear we would be driven to set right what is defiled, to wipe clean what is stained, to heal what is wounded. And so, since we cannot do it with the eyes of the body, let us at least examine ourselves as far as we can with the eyes of the heart, and now set our consciences before the gaze of the inner man. Let us chastise ourselves; let us make a reckoning with ourselves about our daily conduct. Let each soul speak to itself in the secret places of the heart and say: "Let me see whether I have spent this day without sin, without envy, without slander, without grumbling; let me see whether today I have done anything that serves the progress of the soul. I think that today I lied, that I was overcome by anger or by desire, that I did good to no one, and finally that I did not groan for fear of eternal death. Who will give me back this day, which I have wasted on vain things, which I have used up in guilty and most wicked thoughts?"

So then, brothers, let us be pierced with sorrow for all our negligences in our chambers, that is, in our hearts; let us condemn ourselves, let us accuse ourselves daily before our Judge, and while we are in this flesh, let us fight daily against the flesh itself with the Lord's help. Let us overcome our own wills and inclinations until that most longed-for and most blessed time comes to us by the happy change to eternal life, when what the Lord said will be fulfilled: "And men will be like the angels," and again: "Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father."

What, do you suppose, will be the splendor of souls then, when the light of bodies will have the brightness of the sun? For then, when we have come to that blessedness, there will be no sorrow for us, no fear, no death. No weakness will any longer hinder us from serving our Lord, no adversity of fleshly misery will oppose us, nor will any need to fight remain any longer. That time will come, I say, when no refreshment of food or sleep will be desired any more, no weariness from fasting will be felt, no unrest from the flesh or temptation from the enemy will be feared; but with the adversary thrust down into the depths of hell, we shall first enjoy this happiness: that we begin neither to wish to sin any longer nor to be able to. When all wickedness, all misery, all grief have ceased, innocence will possess everything, joy everything, happiness everything. The lesser will fear no misery, the happier will fear no envy, because, with all malice emptied out and utterly extinguished, the love of the angels will pass into human hearts; and mingled with the angels, people, now heavenly, will shine, having received back their flesh without the weakness of the flesh. And so they will never again feel any weariness of the everlasting power of their Lord, nor any flagging in the unending exultation of his praises. We shall have full blessedness amid those immeasurable gifts of our God, so that we shall never tire of giving him thanks, having been made co-heirs of him who said: "Come, you blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world."

See what blessedness will be lost by the one who refuses to amend himself during the time for repentance, who does not redeem himself with his possessions while they are still his own, who, turning remedies into wounds, has bowed his unhappy neck to avarice or to lust. But let us, brothers, with God's help, disdain to serve sins, we for whom such great blessedness is prepared in heaven. So while we may, and while it is in our power, let us reject what is false and passing, so that we may be worthy to receive what is truly good. Let us be emptied of vices and filled with virtues, for no one can take in what is good if he will not free himself from what is evil. Vessels full of mud cannot receive and hold a pure liquid, and a thorny field, unless it has been rooted out by the diligence of its farmers, does not nourish the seed sown in it but chokes it, for it is written that the kindly Holy Spirit will not dwell in a body subject to sins. While we sail in this world as on a stormy sea, so that we may reach our homeland in paradise, let us hasten to bail out the bilge of our vices, so that our soul, adorned with good works like a ship laden with all kinds of goods, may cast anchor in the harbor of eternal blessedness and be worthy to come into the company of the angels, where, set free from the evil report, we may be worthy to hear that happy and longed-for voice: "Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many. Enter into the joy of your Lord." May our Lord Jesus Christ grant this, to whom be honor and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
XIII. A SERMON ON SAINT VINCENT THE MARTYR.

In the account of the passion that was read to us today, dearest brothers, we are plainly shown a savage judge, a bloodthirsty torturer, an unconquered martyr. Though his body was furrowed by many kinds of punishment, the torments gave out while his limbs still held firm. Impiety persisted though refuted by so many miracles; human weakness did not yield though harassed by so many tortures. Let us recognize, then, that it was God's power at work. For how could perishable dust have held out against such monstrous torments unless Christ dwelt in it? In all these things it is he who must be recognized, he who must be glorified, he who must be praised, who gave him faith at his first calling and strength in his final passion. Do you want to know that both were given? Listen to the apostle Paul: "To you," he says, "it has been granted for Christ's sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him." Vincent had received both of these; he had received them and he possessed them. For if he had not received them, what would he have possessed? He had confidence in his speech; he had endurance in his suffering. So let no one rely on his own heart when he speaks, and let no one trust in his own strength when he undergoes temptation, because if we speak good things wisely, our wisdom comes from him, and if we bear evil things bravely, our patience comes from him.

Recall Christ, the Lord of the laws, admonishing his disciples in the Gospel; recall the King of martyrs equipping his cohorts with spiritual weapons, showing them the battles, promising them the rewards. When he had said to his disciples, "In this world you will have tribulation," he at once added something to console their frightened hearts, saying, "But take courage, for I have overcome the world." Why, then, dearest ones, do we wonder that Vincent conquered in him by whom the world was conquered? "In this world," he says, "you will have tribulation," so that, if it presses on you, it may not crush you, and if it attacks you, it may not overthrow you.

The world sends out a double battle line against the soldiers of Christ. Pay attention, brothers. A double battle line, I said, the world sends out against the soldiers of Christ. For it flatters in order to deceive, and it terrifies in order to break. Let our own pleasure not hold us, and let another's cruelty not terrify us. And because Christ meets us at both points of attack, the world is conquered and the Christian is not conquered. If in this passion one considers human endurance, it begins to seem incredible; if one recognizes divine power, it ceases to be astonishing. Such cruelty raged against the martyr's body, and such calm came forth in his voice; such harsh punishments raged in his limbs, and such assurance rang in his words, that one might strangely suppose that while Vincent was suffering someone else was speaking, or at any rate that while Vincent was speaking someone else was being tortured.

And truly, dearest brothers, so it was, it was exactly so. Someone else was speaking. For Christ promised this too to his witnesses. This is how he spoke in the Gospel to his own, whom he was preparing for contests of this kind: "Do not think beforehand how or what you are to speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you." So the flesh suffered and the Spirit spoke, and as the Spirit spoke, not only was impiety refuted but weakness was also strengthened. The torments made the martyr more glorious in our eyes. Pierced by wounds of many kinds, he did not abandon the fight but renewed it more fiercely. You would think the flame was hardening him, not burning him up, and that, like a potter's kiln receiving soft clay, it was turning it into hard earthenware. Our martyr could have said to Dacian: "My flesh no longer cares for your fires, for my strength has dried up like a potsherd." And since it is truly written, "The kiln tests the potter's vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous men," Vincent was tested and fired by that fire, while Dacian burned and crackled. For if he was not burning, where was his smoke coming from? What were the words of that angry man but the smoke of a man on fire? So he applied flames from outside to our martyr, who had refreshment in his heart, while he himself, kindled by the torches of rage, burned within like an oven and was scorching the devil who dwelt in him. For through Dacian's furious shouts, his fierce eyes, his threatening looks and the movements of his whole body, that inner tenant of his was stirring, and through these visible signs he betrayed himself, as through the crackling cracks of the little vessel he had filled. The flame did not torment the martyr as much as madness ravaged the persecutor.

But now, brothers, all that has passed away, both Dacian's anger and Vincent's punishment. Yet Dacian's punishment remains, and Vincent's crown. Indeed, leaving aside for the moment the bounds of the future recompense, to show the glory of the martyrs even in this world: what region, what province overseas, as far as either the empire of the Romans or the Christian name extends, does not rejoice today to celebrate Vincent's feast? And who today would even have heard Dacian's name, had he not read it in the passion of Vincent? And in that the Lord preserved the martyr's body with such care, what else did he show but that he had guided the living man, whom he did not abandon when lifeless? So Vincent defeated Dacian while alive, and he defeats him in death as well. Alive, he trampled on torments; dead, he swam across the seas. But he who among the hooks gave to God an unconquered spirit himself steered the lifeless corpse among the waves. The torturer's flame did not bend his heart, the water of the sea did not sink his body; in all these things there is nothing else but this: "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints." To that glory may the Lord lead us under his protection, to whom be honor and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
XIV. AN ADMONITION.

I ask you, dearest brothers, as I have often urged you, that we strive to think continually of the day of our death and of the terrible and fearful judgment. For no more useful remedies can be found for the wounds of all sins than for each person to think of that hour when he is to depart from this world. For how could it happen that anyone would dare to commit grave sins if he believes that at any moment he may depart from this life? For so Scripture says: "Remember, my son, that death does not delay," and again: "Remember the last things and cease from enmity." For whoever carefully considers how harsh the examination will be before the judgment seat of Christ, where each will receive according to his works, cannot take pleasure in his own sins or crimes. When all nations have been gathered before that dreadful Judge, what weeping of eyes and gnashing of teeth will there be then for the unjust, the adulterers and the greedy, when each of them sees the multitude of the saints set apart at the King's right hand and for glory, and sees the peoples of sin plunged into the depths of Tartarus without end and without any hope of mercy or pardon, shut out in their own darkness from the blessed light of the saints; and when, descending endlessly into the depths, with the pit closing its mouth upon him, he beholds eternal torments and an everlasting death in which he will never die. In vain will he beg mercy from the poor man whom he despised in this life; in vain will he ask, with burning lips, that the tip of Lazarus's finger be laid on them to cool his burning. How the wretch will wish, when he sees the glory of the poor, that he had once been subject to the hard toils of poverty, and had borne in that life evils that would have died along with that life, so as not to deserve to come to those eternal torments!

So then, dearest brothers, that we may not deserve to hear such harsh and terrible things before the judgment seat of the eternal Judge, while we still may, and while with God's help it is in our power, let us examine our consciences. And if we recognize that any crimes or deadly sins not yet cleansed by almsgiving and prayer still hold sway in us, let us hasten, with Christ's help, to overcome the waves of sin and enter the harbor of repentance; and if we recognize that anything in the little ship of our soul has been broken by pride, torn by avarice or loosened by lust in the many storms of sin, let us hasten to set it right and repair it with good works. For past sins do no harm if they no longer please us. Just as no righteous person's righteousness is enough for him unless he perseveres to the end, so no sinner's wickedness can harm him if, before he leaves this body, he takes refuge in the remedy of almsgiving or the medicine of repentance.

But since we cannot know when or at what hour we shall be snatched from this world, let us hasten without any delay or hesitation to flee from the left hand to the right. Do not trust in your health, do not trust in your age. Be always intent on the remedy for your salvation, you who are always uncertain of your life, because he who reassured us by saying, "On whatever day the sinner turns back, all his iniquities will be consigned to oblivion," also wished us to be cautious, saying, "Do not delay to turn to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day."

But perhaps, when we call everyone without distinction to repentance, someone thinks to himself and says: "I am a young man with a wife; how can I cut my hair short or take up the religious habit?" We do not say this, dearest brothers, we do not preach this; rather, young people who are evidently married ought to change their conduct rather than their dress. For what harm does it do a man who has a wife if he resolves to turn his corrupt ways to good and honorable works, if he strives to restore the wounds of his sins to their former health by fasting, prayer and almsgiving? True conversion is sufficient in itself without a change of clothing. But religious clothing without good works not only can provide no remedy but will also incur God's just judgment. Let us therefore turn to better things while the remedies are in our power. Here let us extinguish death by dying to sins; here let us acquire life by the merits of our life, through him who lives and reigns with the Father for ever and ever. Amen.
XV. ON THE LENTEN FAST.

See, dearest brothers, the holy and spiritual days of Lent are now close at hand, days in which the body's losses turn into the soul's gains. And so, since, as the Apostle says, the acceptable time and the days of salvation are coming, let us prepare our minds as if for a spiritual grape harvest, and let us strive to give ourselves to God so fully that in these few days we may gather what will be enough for us for the whole year. For we believe it was of these days that the Lord spoke through the prophet: "On the days of your solemn feasts you shall afflict your souls." Why did he say this? Because fasts and vigils and holy afflictions wear down the humbled body but purify the stained heart; they take strength from the limbs but bring brightness to the conscience. For the weariness of the body redeems the sins of the will; through the discipline of the hard cross, self-indulgence and the pleasures of the flesh are punished. In this way the sentence of future death is appeased by present mortification, and when the author of the fault is humbled, the fault itself is consumed. And while affliction is laid on the body by voluntary discipline, the anger of the dreadful Judge is appeased, and a little labor cancels great sins which eternal fire would scarcely consume. For if we ourselves impose discipline on our sins and spurn the self-indulgence of the flesh through penance, we will quickly make God gracious to us. If you acknowledge your sin, God pardons it. For how could God see fit to pardon a sin that a man does not see fit to acknowledge in himself?

So, as we deal with the matter of our salvation, let us do within ourselves what physicians usually do for our bodies. If some injury or complaint is felt on the surface of the skin, a gentler remedy is applied. But if the wound is hidden in the bones or sunk deep in the inner organs, that hidden force calls for a harsher and more violent remedy, so that the size of the ulcer may be overcome by cautery or by cutting, and pain may be conquered by pain. The same principle must be applied to the sickness of souls. If the sins are perhaps light, for instance if a person has sinned in speech, or by some fault of the will, or with the eye or in the heart, then these stains of words and thoughts may be overcome by daily prayer and must be wiped away by private compunction. But if anyone, questioning his conscience within, has committed some capital crime; if he has assailed and lost his faith by false witness; if he has violated the sacred name of truth by reckless perjury; if he has soiled the snow-white tunic of baptism and the precious silken robe of virginity with the mud of defiled chastity; if he has killed the new man within himself by the crime of murder; if, by observing auguries through soothsayers, diviners and enchanters, he has handed himself over as a captive to the devil: these and similar evils can scarcely be fully expiated by ordinary, moderate or private satisfaction. Grave cases require graver, sharper and public remedies, so that one who has ruined himself to the destruction of many may in the same way redeem himself to the edification of many. For a man deceives himself if, when he feels the disease burning deep within his marrow, he spreads a soothing ointment over the surface of his body.

These capital evils, then, call for great roaring and groaning and a fountain of tears, and we must cry out with the prophet: "I roared from the groaning of my heart," and: "Every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears," and again: "I ate ashes like bread and mingled my drink with weeping." Let no one despise penance; let no one scorn this humility. For it was a king, David, who said these things; it was a supreme king who did them. So we must raise loud cries and great lamentation over a soul killed by sins, as over the dead. And just as a bereaved mother laments with a broken heart over the loss of her only son, so it is fitting for us to grieve over our only soul, yet with hope of its restoration. Of this only one the prophetic word says: "Deliver my soul from the sword, and my only one from the hand of the dog." Why does he say "only one"? Either because it must be loved as one's only one, or because it alone, stripped of every consolation, will have to give an account before the judgment seat of Christ. So, I say, over this only one, slain by the sword of crimes, the whole weight of grief must be poured out with roaring and groaning, in case it can perhaps be revived by the warm compresses of tears and the heat of faith. Compunction must be kindled, and prayers must be strengthened by remembering the judgment to come. And we must listen to the counsel of the prophet Daniel, but listen with the ear of obedience, when he says: "O king, accept my counsel, and redeem your sins by alms to the poor." We must also listen to the example of that man in the Gospel as if it were truly written for our redemption: "See, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor." Of these poor we have heard the Lord say in the Gospel, with inexpressible condescension and love: "Whoever has done it to one of these least ones has done it to me." These words commend to us, with heavenly authority, the fruits of almsgiving.

But perhaps, when we speak of alms, those in narrow poverty will be alarmed and say that they have nothing to give to the poor. Yet no one will be able to excuse himself on this ground, since the Lord promised that he would give a reward even for a cup of cold water, and he praised the widow who had put two coins into the treasury. For our God is fed not by the size of the gift but by the goodwill of the giver.

For my part, beloved, I think that our Lord allowed the poor to exist in this world so that through the poor he might test the faith of the rich, or show mercy to the rich through their mercy to the poor; so that those who have plenty might not lack an opportunity for good works and for their own redemption; so that even another's need might enrich the kind and merciful; so that every wealthier person might gain great profit from the needy, and by a wonderful and most excellent exchange, while giving mercy to the poor through a temporary gift, might thereby acquire eternal treasures for himself. Let us direct our actions so that whatever we can, whatever we are able, we may devote, for love of eternal life, to the practice of goodwill and to the pursuit of justice and mercy. Let us run while we have the light, before darkness overtakes us, for in that world it will no longer be possible to look to amendment and redemption, as the divine word says: "For in death there is no one who remembers you." Just as there no loss of merits will any longer be feared, so no forgiveness of sins will be granted; no freedom to do good works will be allowed there any more.

So, brothers, reflecting on these things wisely and to our good, let us hasten to take refuge in the remedies of penance, and through chastity and humility, through works of justice and mercy, let us gain for ourselves eternal rewards with God, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
XVI. ON THE SUNDAY AT THE BEGINNING OF LENT

Our Lord and Savior urges and admonishes us through the prophet how we ought to come to him after much negligence, saying: "Come, let us worship and fall down before the Lord who made us," and again: "Turn to me with your whole heart, with fasting, weeping and mourning." For the days of holy Lent, dearest brothers, if we consider them carefully, signify the life of this present world, just as the days of Easter prefigure eternal blessedness. And just as in Lent we have a kind of sorrow so that at Easter we may rejoice in due order, so in this world, as long as we live, we ought to do penance, so that in the world to come we may receive forgiveness of our sins and attain eternal joy. But each person should sigh over his sins, shed tears and give alms in such a way that, with God's help, he always strives to avoid those sins for as long as he lives. For just as no one ever has been or ever could be without small sins, so, by God's gift and help, we ought to be entirely free of capital crimes.

And so that we may achieve this, if at other times the hindrances of the world keep us bound, then at least in the days of holy Lent let us meditate on the law of the Lord day and night, as it is written, and let us so fill our hearts with the sweetness of the divine law that we leave no place in us empty of virtues for vices to occupy. For just as at the time of the harvest and the grape harvest, dearest brothers, people gather what will sustain our flesh, so in the days of Lent, as in a time of spiritual harvest and vintage, let us gather what will enable our soul to live for ever. For just as a careless man who gathers nothing at harvest or vintage will be tormented by hunger throughout the whole year, so whoever neglects in this season to provide and gather spiritual wheat and heavenly wine into the barns of his soul, by fasting, reading and praying, will endure the harshest thirst and cruel want for ever.

Know most certainly, dearest brothers, that a soul which is not continually fed with the word of God is like flesh that receives food only after many days. And just as the flesh becomes thin and dry through hunger and want, like a kind of ghost, so the soul too, if it is not fed with the food of God's word, is found parched and useless and fit for no good work. Consider, dearest brothers: every year we get ready the granary, the wine store and the pantry, so that our flesh may have food for one year. How much, do you suppose, ought we to lay up so that our soul may be sustained for ever? And so, dearest brothers, at least for these few days let the hindrances of the world withdraw, since, according to Scripture, they make many careless people wretched. Let carnal merriment withdraw; let the poison-filled allurements of this world withdraw. Let the pleasures of the flesh be lessened, so that the gains of the soul may be spiritually prepared, because of what is written: "Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep," and: "Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted." Let the time that the frenzied game of dice used to take from us begin to be filled with divine reading, and in place of hateful gossip, biting jokes and poisonous slander let there be conversation about the holy Scriptures. In the hours in which we used to be taken up with hunting, to the harm of our souls, let the sick be visited, those in prison be sought out, strangers be welcomed, and those at odds be called back to harmony.

If we do these things, brothers, we can prepare remedies for ourselves from the very sources from which we had inflicted wounds on ourselves. Above all, on fast days let us give to the poor what we used to eat at midday, so that no one tries to prepare costly suppers and banquets of exquisite flavors for himself and seems to have merely shifted his body's abundance of food rather than reduced it. It does no good to have kept a long fast all day if afterward the soul is overwhelmed by the delicacy or excess of food. For the mind that is filled with such things grows foul, and the soil of our body, once watered, will sprout the thorns of lust. So let our food be moderate, let the stomach never be overfilled, and let us always think more about the food of the heart than about the food of the body, since inwardly, in the inner man, we were made in the image of God, while in the flesh we were formed from the clay of the earth. And see, brothers, whether it is right that the flesh, made from earth, should sometimes take food twice a day, while the soul, which is the image of God, scarcely receives the word of God after several days, when it is surely to our advantage to honor the image of God in us more than our flesh. For those who think only of the flesh are like beasts and cattle, and those who act so have already crushed the image of God within themselves. Let the flesh be governed like a maidservant, and let the soul be preferred as the rightful mistress. If it is otherwise, if we do not recognize that we were made in the image of God and think more about the flesh than about the soul, I fear the Holy Spirit may rebuke us through the prophet, saying: "Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he has been compared to senseless beasts and has become like them."

Listen gladly to the divine readings in church, as you are accustomed, and read them again in your homes. If anyone is so busy that he cannot apply himself to the divine Scriptures before his meal, let him not be reluctant to read something from the divine Scriptures at his table, so that, as the flesh is fed with food, the soul may be refreshed with the word of God, and the whole person, that is, the outer and the inner, may rise satisfied from a holy and wholesome banquet. For if only the flesh is fed and the soul is not refreshed with the word of God, the maidservant is filled while the mistress is tormented by hunger. How unjust this is, your holiness cannot fail to see. And so, as I have already said, you ought to hear and read the divine readings with such eagerness that you can also speak about them and teach others in your homes and elsewhere, wherever you may be; and like clean animals, chewing over the word of God in constant reflection, you can take in its useful juice, that is, its spiritual meaning, for yourselves, and with God's help offer it to others to drink. So you will fulfill what is written: "And your cup that inebriates, how excellent it is!" and fulfill what the blessed Apostle urges and admonishes, saying: "Whether you eat or drink or do anything else, do all things for the glory of God." And if illness does not prevent you, fast every day and rise for the vigils with eager and fervent devotion, because of what is written: "Day and night my spirit keeps watch for you, O God," and again: "To you, Lord, I will pray in the morning, and you will hear my voice," and again: "At midnight I rose to give praise to your name, Lord." To this our Lord and Savior also urges and admonishes us in the Gospel, saying: "Watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation." May he deign to grant this, to whom be honor and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.
XVII. ON THE GOSPEL READING WHERE IT SAYS: "DO NOT LET YOUR LEFT HAND KNOW WHAT YOUR RIGHT HAND IS DOING"

The Gospel reading that has just been read to us, dearest brothers, seems to me impossible to understand according to the letter, and so, with God's help, let us look for a way to reach its spiritual meaning. For it says: "Take care not to practice your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them," and again: "When you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing," whereas elsewhere it says: "Let your light so shine before people that they may see your good works." Pay careful attention, brothers, and seek the understanding of divine Scripture humbly and wisely. For the Lord cannot contradict himself in the Gospel reading. Since he himself said that alms should be given in secret and he himself urged that they be given publicly, a sober understanding is needed so that his commands do not seem to contradict each other. Whoever gives alms because he wants to be praised by people is acting publicly even if he gives in secret, because he is seeking praise from people. But whoever gives alms solely for the love of God, so that others may imitate him in good works and so that not he but the Lord may be praised, is acting in secret even if he gives alms publicly, because in return for that alms he desires not what is seen but what is not seen, and he wishes to receive not praise from people but a reward from God.

We should understand fasting in the same way. For since the Lord himself says, "Anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not be seen by people to be fasting," are we then acting against Christ's commands when we proclaim a fast publicly and fast together with the whole people looking on? It must be understood in this sense: that no one should fast for human praise, but for the forgiveness of sins and for God's mercy. Therefore let each person question his conscience, and if he gives alms for God alone, let him give them confidently and publicly, so that whoever sees him may imitate him. For the Lord's saying, "Do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing," is also seen to concern what we said above. By the right hand is understood the love of God; by the left, the vanity or greed of the world. If you give alms for human praise, the left hand does it all and the right hand nothing at all. But if you give alms for the forgiveness of sins and for love of eternal life, the right hand does it all. What then does "Do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing" mean, except that the vanity or greed of the world should not corrupt or destroy what the love of God does? For if anyone believes this can be fulfilled according to the letter, what will he do if his right hand is hurt? Must he not give alms with his left? Or if he wants to ransom a captive, how will he be able to open his chest or untie his purse unless he joins his left hand to his right? Or if he has to welcome a stranger and, according to the Lord's command, wash the feet of the saints, I do not see how he can do this without his left hand knowing.

To this also belongs what the Lord said: "Do not pray on the street corners, but go into your room," he says, "shut the door, and pray to your Father in secret." You yourselves recognize well that this too cannot always be fulfilled according to the letter. For we ourselves and the whole people not only pray in our rooms but also gather in church and kneel together with all the people. In doing this, are we acting against the commands of Christ, who said that we ought to pray in our rooms with the door shut? Not at all. So this meaning too agrees with the earlier saying. Pay careful attention, then, to how this should be understood. Whenever you pray to God and ask him for what is seen, you are praying publicly and with the door open, because you want to receive from God what is seen. But if you wish to pray for the forgiveness of sins and for eternal life, even if you pray publicly, you are praying with the door shut, because you are asking not for what is seen but for what is not seen. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal. If you seek temporal things, as I said above, you pray publicly and with the door open; if you seek eternal things, your prayer is secret, because you wish to receive not what is seen but what is not seen. So whoever seeks in truth the things that are not seen will also receive the things that are seen, as the Lord's reward, for he does not lie who says: "Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you."

We do not say this, brothers, to keep us from praying to the Lord for temporal things, that is, for bodily health, for peace among peoples, or for abundant crops. We ought to ask God for these things too, but in second and third place, so that in the whole aim of our prayer the first place is held by love of the soul and desire for eternal life. Let us pray for the body, but let us make supplication incomparably more for the soul. And so, dearest brothers, whenever this Gospel reading is read to you, you should take its meaning in the way we have suggested above, so that, whether in almsgiving or in fasting or in prayer, whether with the right hand or with the left, we may strive to observe this: that whatever we do, we do not for the vanity or greed of the world but for love of eternal blessedness. May he deign to grant this, who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.
XVIII. ON THE CALLING OF ABRAHAM

Just now, when the divine reading was read, we heard the Lord saying to blessed Abraham: "Go out," he says, "from your land and from your kindred and from your father's house." For everything, dearest brothers, that was written in the Old Testament held up beforehand a type and an image of the New Testament. So too the apostle Paul says: "For all these things happened to them in figure. But they were written for our sake, upon whom the end of the ages has come." If, then, they were written for our sake, the things we read were done bodily in Abraham at that time we see fulfilled spiritually in ourselves, if we live holy and upright lives. "Go out," he says, "from your land and from your kindred and from your father's house." All these things, dearest brothers, we both believe and feel to be fulfilled in us through the sacrament of baptism. Our land is our flesh. We go out well from our land when we abandon fleshly habits and keep close to the footsteps of Christ. Does it not seem to you that a man goes out happily from his land, that is, from himself, when from proud he becomes humble, patient instead of wrathful, chaste instead of lustful, generous instead of greedy, kind instead of envious, gentle instead of bloodthirsty?

Truly, dearest brothers, he goes out happily from his land who is changed in this way for the love of God. Indeed, even in private conversation we are accustomed to speak like this: if some wicked man suddenly begins to do good works, we say of him, "That man has gone out of himself." And truly he is rightly said to have gone out of himself who has rejected vices and delights in virtues. "Go out," says the Lord, "from your land." Our land, that is, our flesh, was before baptism the land of the dying; after baptism it has become the land of the living. This is the land of which the prophet had sung, saying: "I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living." Through baptism, then, as I have said, we have become a land of the living and not of the dying, that is, of virtues and not of vices, provided that after receiving baptism we do not return to the wallowing-mire of vices, and that after becoming a land of the living we do not do works that are lustful and liable to death. "And come," says the Lord, "into the land that I will show you." For we shall come with joy to the land that the Lord shows us only if first, with his help, we drive vices and sins out of our land, that is, out of our flesh. "Go out," he says, "from your kindred." This kindred is understood as the vices and sins that are in a certain way born with us in part, and are nourished from infancy by evil habits. We go out from our kindred, then, when through the grace of baptism we are emptied of all sins and vices, yet in such a way that afterwards, with God's help, we labor as much as we can so that, the vices having been driven out, we may be filled with virtues. For if, after being emptied of all evils in baptism, we choose to be idle and sluggish, I fear that there may be fulfilled in us what is written in the Gospel: "When the unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he walks through dry places seeking rest and does not find it. Afterwards, returning, if he finds the house empty, he will bring with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and the last state of that man will be worse than the first."

So, then, let us go out from our kindred, that is, from sins and vices, in such a way that we never afterwards wish to return to these evils like a dog to its vomit. "Go out," says the Lord, "also from your father's house." This too, dearest brothers, we ought to take spiritually. Before the grace of Christ, our father was the devil. Of him the Lord says in the Gospel, rebuking the Jews: "You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father." He called the devil the father of men, then, not because they were born of him but because they imitated his wickedness; not because they could be born of him, but because they chose to imitate him. For that the devil was formerly our father the psalmist recalls, speaking in the person of God addressing the Church: "Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father's house." Consider first, then, what he said: "Hear, daughter," he says. He who says "Hear, daughter" is certainly a father. When he said, "Forget your people and your father's house," he is certainly warning that a father must be left behind. We are invited, then, by God the Father to leave the devil as our father through a blessed and happy exchange. We leave the devil as father well if, with God's help, we always strive to avoid or flee his cunning and wickedness.

All these things, then, that we may go out from our land, that is, from fleshly living, and leave our kindred, that is, vices and sins, and escape from the house of our father the devil, we have been granted not by our own strength but by the gift of Christ's grace. And therefore let us labor as much as we can, with God's help, not to return again to fellowship or friendship with the devil, or to vices, or to fleshly desires, because of what is written: "Now you have been made well; do not sin, lest something worse happen to you." Rather, by imitating Abraham's faith and constantly doing good works, may we attain not only pardon but also fellowship and friendship with God. We ought also, with great fear and trembling, to consider and dread what the Lord said to Moses on this same matter. For he speaks thus: "When the Lord has handed over to you the land of the Canaanites, take care never to make friendships with the inhabitants of that land, which would be your ruin." Since we believe that through the grace of baptism all crimes and sins have been driven out of us, if afterwards we make friendships with those very vices and sins by consenting to them in greed or lust, without doubt their friendship becomes our ruin.

And therefore let us labor as much as we can, with God's help, for the salvation of the soul, and let us hasten to bring virtues into the field of our heart, which sins and crimes were accustomed to occupy, so that there may be fulfilled in us what blessed Isaac, as a type of Christ, said when blessing his son: "See, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed." May he deign to grant this, to whom be honor and dominion with the Father in the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.
19. ON ABRAHAM AND ISAAC HIS SON.

That reading, dearest brothers, in which blessed Abraham is read to have offered his son Isaac as a burnt offering, is not recited in its proper order during the days of Lent because, as you yourselves know, it is reserved for the Easter vigil on account of the sacrament of the Lord's passion. And since there is no time then to say anything about it, now, if you so wish, let us set before the ears of your charity, as briefly as we can, an exposition of it according to the way our fathers treated it under the Lord's inspiration.

The Lord said, then, to Abraham: "Take your son Isaac, whom you love, and offer him to me as a burnt offering on one of the mountains that I will show you." And he rose, saddled his donkey, took with him two servants and his son Isaac, and came on the third day to the place that the Lord had shown him. For Abraham, when he offered his son Isaac, bore the type of God the Father, while Isaac bore the figure of the Lord and Savior. And that the place of sacrifice is reached on the third day shows forth the mystery of the Trinity. For that the third day ought to be taken as a sacrament or mystery of the Trinity is frequently found in the sacred books, as in Exodus: "We will go a three days' journey into the wilderness"; and again, when they came to Mount Sinai, the people were told: "Sanctify yourselves and be ready for the third day"; and Joshua, when about to cross the Jordan, warned the people to be ready on the third day; and the Lord rose on the third day. We have said this because blessed Abraham came on the third day to the place that the Lord had shown him.

The two servants whom Abraham ordered to stay behind with the donkey bore the type of the Jewish people, who, because they were not going to believe in Christ, could not go up to or reach the place where he was to be sacrificed. That donkey signifies the synagogue, while the ram that was held by its horns among the thorns also seems to have borne the type of the Lord. For Christ too clung, as it were by his horns, among thorns when he hung on the horns of the cross, fastened by the nails. And in that Isaac himself carried the wood for his own sacrifice, in this too he prefigured Christ the Lord, who himself carried his cross to the place of his passion. Of this mystery it had been said through the prophet long before: "And his government shall be upon his shoulders." For Christ had the government upon his shoulders when he carried his cross with wonderful humility. Not unfittingly does the cross of Christ signify government, for through it the devil is conquered and the whole world is called back to the knowledge and grace of Christ. Thus Paul too said, when speaking of the Lord's passion: "He became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name."

We have said this, brothers, so that your charity may recognize that the government of Christ, of which it is written, "And his government shall be upon his shoulders," is nothing other than his cross. And that is why that reading is read at Easter, when the true Isaac, whose type the son of Abraham bore, is fastened to the gibbet of the cross for the human race. We also read in that same reading that blessed Abraham, coming with his son, saw the place from afar and said to the servants: "Sit here with the donkey. I and the boy will go on, and when we have worshiped we will return to you." Why is it said to the servants, who bore the figure of the Jews, "Sit here with the donkey"? Could that donkey sit, brothers? But it is said, "Sit with the donkey," because the Jewish people, who were not going to believe in Christ, could not stand, but, being weak and as it were sick with sin, having scorned the staff of the cross, were going to fall to the ground. So blessed Abraham says: "Sit here with the donkey; I and the boy will go on, and when we have worshiped we will return to you." What is this you say, blessed Abraham? You are going to sacrifice your son, and you say you will return with your son? For if you offer him as a burnt offering, he certainly cannot come back with you. Blessed Abraham could have answered: "I speak the truth: I am offering my son, and I will return with my son to you. So great is my faith that I believe that he who deigned to give him to me from a barren mother can also raise him from the dead; and therefore I speak the truth when I say that when we have worshiped we will return to you."

That the ram was killed and Isaac was not killed happened because Isaac was the figure and not the reality; and so in him was marked out what was afterwards fulfilled in Christ. See the Lord contending with men in great loving-kindness. Abraham offered to God a mortal son who was not going to die, and God handed over to death an immortal Son for the sake of men. Yet blessed Isaac and that ram can also be understood in this way: that in blessed Isaac the divinity of Christ is signified, and in the ram his humanity. And because we believe that in the passion it was not the divinity but the humanity that was crucified, therefore it is not Isaac but the ram that is sacrificed. For the only-begotten of God is offered, and the firstborn of the Virgin is sacrificed.

Hear another sacrament, dearest brothers. Blessed Jerome the priest wrote that he had learned with complete certainty from ancient and elder Jews that Isaac was offered in the very place where Christ was later crucified. Indeed, from the place from which blessed Abraham was commanded to set out, one reaches on the third day the place where Christ was crucified. It is also handed down by the report of the ancients that Adam, the first man, was once buried in the very place where the cross was set up, and that it was called the place of the skull because the first head of the human race is said to have been buried there. And truly, brothers, it is not unfitting to believe that the physician was raised up where the sick man lay. And it was fitting that where human pride had fallen, there divine mercy should stoop down, and that that precious blood, as it deigned to drip down and touch even bodily the dust of the ancient sinner, should be believed to have redeemed it. These things, dearest brothers, we have gathered as best we could from various books of the Scriptures for the progress of your souls, and have offered them out of regard for your charity. But you, with the Lord's help, as you reread the divine Scriptures more often, if you attend carefully, will, I believe, be able to find an even better exposition.

I ask you, brothers, that whoever wishes his son or his household servant to be baptized should not put off presenting him to the church now, because it is not right that a thing believed to be so great and so glorious should be sought carelessly or later than is fitting. For I fear that some women present their little children late precisely because they are unwilling to come to the vigils with them. For we believe most certainly that those who are willing to present those who are to be baptized as soon as Lent begins, and who faithfully come with them to the vigils, and whose children receive the sacrament of baptism in the proper order, will themselves also obtain the forgiveness of sins, by the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.
20. ON SAINT JOSEPH, I.

Whenever readings from the Old Testament are recited to you, dearly beloved, as I have often reminded you, you ought to attend not only to what sounds in the words but to what is understood and savored in the spirit. So too the apostle admonishes us, saying: "The letter kills, but the spirit gives life." For all these things that are read in the Old Testament, as the apostle says, happened to them in figure, but they were written for our sake. For when the Christian people come faithfully to church, what does it profit them to hear how the holy patriarchs took wives or begot sons, unless they perceive with a spiritual understanding why these things were done or what they prefigured? See, we have heard that blessed Jacob begot a son and called his name Joseph, and loved him more than his other sons. In this passage blessed Jacob bore the figure of God the Father, and holy Joseph bore the type of the Lord and Savior. Jacob loved his son, and God the Father loved his only Son. Jacob sent his son to look after his brothers, and God the Father sent his only-begotten Son to visit the human race, sick with sins. Joseph, while seeking his brothers, wandered in the wilderness; and Christ sought the human race, which was wandering in the world, so that in the world he too was, as it were, wandering, because he was seeking the wanderers. Joseph sought his brothers in Shechem. Shechem means "shoulder." For sinners always turn their back to the face of the righteous, and the shoulders are at the back. For just as Joseph's brothers, struck with envy, turned their back rather than their face to brotherly love, so too the unhappy Jews chose to envy rather than to love the author of salvation when he came to them. Of such it is said in the psalm: "Let their eyes be darkened so that they do not see, and bow down their back always."

Joseph found his brothers in Dothan. Dothan means "failing." Truly they were in great failing who were contemplating the murder of a brother. So when his brothers saw Joseph, they plotted his death. In the same way, when they saw the true Joseph, Jesus Christ, they all resolved with one counsel to crucify him. As his brothers stripped Joseph of his many-colored, ankle-length robe, so the Jews stripped Christ of the tunic of his body through death on the cross. Joseph, stripped of his tunic, is thrown into a cistern, that is, into a pit; and Christ, stripped of human flesh, descended into hell. Joseph, after he is lifted out of the cistern, is sold to the Ishmaelites, that is, to the Gentiles; and Christ, after he returns from hell, is purchased by all the nations through the commerce of faith. Joseph is sold off for thirty pieces of silver on the advice of Judah, and Christ is sold in the same way on the advice of Judas Iscariot. And that in different translations Joseph is not written to have been sold for the same price, but some have said twenty pieces of silver and others thirty, spiritually signified that Christ would not be believed in or loved equally by all. Indeed, even now in the Church some love him more and others less. Christ is worth more to the one who loves him with greater charity. Joseph went down into Egypt, and Christ into the world. Joseph saves Egypt from want of grain, and Christ frees the world from hunger for the word of God. For had his brothers not sold Joseph, Egypt would have perished; and it is true, brothers, that had the Jews not crucified Christ, the world would have perished.

Yet let us see, dearest brothers, why his brothers raged so cruelly against blessed Joseph. Why, if not from the poison of envy, through which death entered the world? Indeed, hear the Scripture saying: "His brothers envied him and could not speak a peaceable word to him." For blessed Joseph had seen a dream, as if he were standing with his brothers in a field gathering sheaves, and the eleven sheaves of his brothers bowed down to his sheaf. This was fulfilled in that Joseph when his brothers bowed down to him in Egypt. And not unfittingly were the barren sheaves compelled to bow down to the fruitful sheaf through which they were to be delivered from the danger of famine.

He also saw another dream, that the sun and the moon and eleven stars bowed down to him. His father answered him: "Shall I and your mother and your brothers bow down to you on the earth?" This could not be fulfilled in that Joseph, because his mother had already departed this life. But in our Joseph, that is, our Lord Jesus Christ, the sacraments of that dream were fulfilled. For the sun and the moon and eleven stars bowed down to him when, after the resurrection, holy Mary, as the moon, and blessed Joseph, with the eleven stars, that is, the blessed apostles, worshiped him, bowing and prostrating themselves before him; and the prophecy was fulfilled that had said: "Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all you stars and light." For how could it suit his brothers that they should worship him as stars, when the night of envy had made them dark and gloomy? They had already lost the brightness of stars who had extinguished in themselves the light of charity. Rightly, then, do we believe that this was more truly fulfilled in our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, whom, as I said before, we read that blessed Joseph and blessed Mary with the eleven apostles frequently worshiped. For that the apostles had the light of stars the Lord himself said in the Gospel: "You are the light of the world"; and again, of them and those like them: "Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father."

Joseph means "increase" or "enlargement." But in that Joseph only Egypt received enlargement, whereas in our Joseph the whole world was found worthy to receive increase. That Joseph distributed wheat; ours deigned to distribute the word of God. "For their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world." We, then, dearest brothers, who with no preceding merits have obtained such great goods through the mercy of the true Joseph, our Lord Jesus Christ, and to whom not the shadow of the Old Testament but the truth itself has come, let us labor as much as we can, with God's grace, so that what he bestowed on us when he was judged he may find intact in us when he comes to judge; for as much as he has bestowed on you, so much will he demand back. And indeed, when he comes, he will render what he promised, but he will also seek those whom he redeemed, and what he gave at his first coming he will exact at his second. Let no one, then, repay Christ our Lord evil for good. For who acts so impiously, if not the one who receives sweetness and gives back bitterness, who receives life and returns death? For he repays death who kills himself by living wickedly. For who repays evil for good, if not the one who, when he ought to devote himself to reading and hasten to church, chooses instead to play at dice and to frequent shows that are frenzied or bloody or shameful; and who, when he ought to wear away his sins by praying, reading, and giving alms, strives instead to increase them and heap them up still more? Who is it that repays evil for good? The one who returns darkness for light, malice for kindness, drunkenness for sobriety, plunder for almsgiving, iniquity for justice.

Whoever, then, with our Lord's help, has not committed these evils, let him guard the divine gifts in himself as best he can. But whoever feels himself guilty of these evils and understands that he is entangled in them, let him quickly run back to the medicines of penance and, before that darkened soul departs from the body of its death, let him obtain for himself a remedy for the day of need through almsgiving, fasting, and prayer. Let us act thus, then, brothers, so that before the judgment seat of Christ those who are good may obtain a crown, and those who are negligent, pardon.
21. ON SAINT JOSEPH, II.

Dearest brothers, anyone who looks carefully at the blessed Jacob and at his holy son Joseph will see that the Lord did something truly wonderful in them. First, I do not think it was without reason that God, who had so often deigned to show himself to the blessed Jacob, chose for so many years not to reveal to him that his son Joseph was alive, and instead let him waste away in long grief. If anyone thinks this happened without a clear and definite reason, let him at least consider this: Joseph his son, though he was so close by, was not allowed to send word to his father that he was not only alive but also placed in high honour. From the place where the blessed Jacob lived to Egypt was scarcely three hundred miles, and a great many people constantly travelled from Egypt to the places where Jacob was. Endless crowds kept streaming from that region into Egypt. But perhaps someone will say that the blessed Joseph left his father when he was a little child and so could not remember him. That is not so, dearest brothers. He was a boy, but sixteen years old, and he could in no way have forgotten his parents. Indeed, he had forgotten them so little that he recognized his brothers the moment he saw them.

But someone says that he did not have the permission or the power to send to his homeland. Even if that seemed somewhat plausible, after he was brought out of prison and made lord over all the land of Egypt, through those seven years of plenty and the two that passed in the time of famine before his brothers came down to him, through those nine years he could without any doubt have sent to his father over three hundred miles. But by a hidden judgment the Lord did not allow this to happen, so much so that Joseph did not reveal himself to his brothers even when they had come to buy grain. On the contrary, he spoke to them very harshly, kept their brother in chains, and ordered them to return to their father in great sorrow.

Notice yet another and greater wonder. See how the blessed Joseph, who knew that his father was suffering unbearable bitterness on his account, as if what he had already endured were too little, had Benjamin taken away as well, knowing full well that this would cause him manifold grief. I do not believe that all this happened without the ordering of the Holy Spirit. For God, whose judgments are often hidden but never unjust, who would not reveal to the blessed Jacob that his son was alive, also did not permit the holy Joseph to announce his glory to his father; on the contrary, by keeping Simeon in chains and taking Benjamin away, he heaped up his own father's distress. Yet if we consider these things faithfully, dearest brothers, we shall recognize that the Lord did them with great mercy. For from the beginning of the world God has done in his saints what he accomplished with great kindness in the blessed Jacob.

But pay careful attention to why this was done. Although the servants and friends of God have avoided deadly crimes and done many good works, we do not believe they have been without small sins, for he does not lie who said: "No one is free from sin, not even an infant whose life on earth is but one day." And the blessed John the Evangelist, who was certainly not inferior in merit to holy Job, cried out and said: "If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us"; and there is what is written elsewhere: "The righteous man falls seven times a day and rises again." Since, then, as has been said, Jacob could not be without these small sins, God, wishing to burn up the small sins in this saint by the fire of tribulation, fulfils in him what he himself said through the Holy Spirit: "The furnace tests the potter's vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous men"; and also: "God scourges every son whom he loves"; and: "Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God." So, in order that our God might present the holy Jacob at the coming judgment like refined gold, he first wiped away from him every stain of sin, so that the fire that is to judge could find nothing in him to burn.

If we pay careful attention, dearest brothers, we see that what we believe God did toward the blessed Jacob, Joseph also did toward his brothers. He was certainly so holy that he could not have hated them. So we must believe that he wore them down with tribulations in order to move them to confess their crime and to take the remedy of repentance. And indeed, in great sorrow they said that they deserved to suffer these things, because they had sinned against their brother when they saw his distress. And because the blessed Joseph knew that the crime of fratricide could not be forgiven his brothers without great repentance, he refined them once, twice and a third time in healing tribulation as in a spiritual fire, not to avenge himself but to correct them. Indeed, until they confessed their sin and wore away the crime they had committed by reproaching one another, he neither let them recognize him nor granted them the kiss of peace. But when he saw them humbly afflicted for the sin they had committed against him, he kissed each of them and wept, and, bathing the necks of the frightened men with the tender dew of his eyes, he washed away his brothers' hatred with tears of love.

What God did in the blessed Jacob, then, and what Joseph did toward his brothers, we too must carry out toward those who have sinned against us: we should take care to hate not them but their sins, and be willing to correct them with the severe chastisement their fault deserves, while taking care to love them in truth. If we do this, dearest brothers, there is fulfilled in us what is written: "Bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ."

Finally, to sum up all I have said in a few words: let us forgive those who have sinned against us in the way we want God to forgive us whenever we sin against him. If we do this, we can say without fear: "Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors."

We would still be glad to say something more to you, beloved, about the blessed Joseph, but for the sake of the poor, who are hurrying to their work, it is better that we keep it for tomorrow. So let us turn to the Lord and beg his mercy, that he may deign always to increase and preserve the desire to hear the word of God which in his kindness he has granted us, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.
22. ON SAINT JOSEPH, III.

Now receive, attentive and in silence and quiet as is your custom, what we kept back for you, beloved, from yesterday's sermon on the blessed Joseph. Dearly beloved brothers, in order to rule the kingdom of Egypt with wonderful wisdom, the blessed Joseph first ruled himself. Though he was handsome and fair of face, he did not turn the beauty of his countenance to another's harm, but kept it for his own grace. He judged that he would be the more beautiful if he showed himself fairer not by the loss of chastity but by the cultivation of modesty, and that true beauty is the kind that does not snare other people's eyes or wound weak minds. The crime was his mistress's, who looked wrongly, not the blessed Joseph's, who did not want to be looked at wrongly. Nor is there any fault in his having been seen. It was not in a slave's power to avoid being seen by his mistress; it was the husband who should have guarded his wife's eyes. Yet let men too learn to beware of women's eyes: even a man who did not want to be loved can be desired. Indeed Joseph was desired, though he would spurn the one who desired him, and Scripture rightly excuses him when it says: "His master's wife cast her eyes on Joseph." That is, he did not show himself off or ensnare her unawares; she cast her own nets and was caught in her own toils; she scattered her own snares and was bound in her own bonds. And she said to him: "Lie with me." The adulteress's first darts are those of the eyes, the second those of words. But one who is not captured by the eyes can resist words. He is excused for having gone in; he is praised for having escaped, and he did not value the garments of his body above the chastity of his soul. He left behind, as if they were not his, the things the adulteress held in her hands, and he judged to be foreign to him whatever could be grasped by the touch of a shameless woman. He was plainly a great man: though sold as a slave, he knew nothing of a slave's character. Desired, he did not desire in return; asked, he did not consent; seized, he fled. When his master's wife accosted him, he could be held by his garment, but he could not be captured in his spirit. He did not even endure her words for long, judging that he would be infected if he stayed any longer, lest the incitements of lust pass to him through the adulteress's hands; and so he went out without his garment. He shook off the crime, and leaving behind the clothes by which he was being held, he fled stripped indeed but not naked, for he was better covered by the garment of modesty. For no one is naked except the one whom guilt has stripped.

Indeed, we have it earlier in Scripture that Adam, after he abandoned God's command by transgression and took on the heavier heat of sin, was naked, and so he himself says: "I heard your voice in paradise and was afraid, because I am naked, and I hid myself." He understood that he was naked because he had lost the adornment of divine protection, and so he hid, that is, because he no longer had the garment of faith, which he had of course laid aside by transgressing. You see a great thing here. The one who did not lose his tunic was naked; the one who took off his garments and left them in the adulteress's hands was not naked. Scripture declares Adam naked; it did not say that Joseph was naked. So Joseph rather stripped himself than made himself naked, for he kept the garments of the virtues uncorrupted, putting off the old man with his deeds in order to put on the new man, who is kept [?] for knowledge according to the image of the Creator. But Adam remained naked, for he could not clothe himself again. Stripped of the power of his singular privilege, he then received a tunic of skins, because as a sinner he could not have a spiritual one.

When Joseph was accused, in all his answers he would not call her guilty, for a righteous man does not know how to accuse, and so the shameless woman did this with impunity. I would say, then, that she was truly the one stripped, even while holding Joseph's human cloak, for she had lost all the ornaments of modesty and of chastity of soul [?]. I would say that he was well adorned and well clothed, whose voice was not heard while his innocence spoke. So later Susanna, keeping silent at her trial, spoke better than any oracle, and so she earned a prophet's defence, since she did not seek the help of her own voice. I would call him more blessed, then, when he was sent to prison, for he was enduring martyrdom for chastity. The gift of purity is good even when it is kept without danger, but when it is defended at the risk of one's life, then it is crowned more fully. Without a hearing, Joseph is sent to prison as though guilty of a crime, but the Lord did not desert him even in prison. It is no disgrace for the innocent when they are attacked with false charges, when justice is crushed and they are handed over to prison. The Lord visits his own even in prison, and so there is more danger there [?]. But what wonder is it if Christ visits those in prison, when he said that he himself had been shut up in prison in the person of his own, as you have it written: "I was in prison and you did not come to me"?

Where does divine mercy not reach? Joseph found such favour that he who had been shut up in prison became instead the keeper of the prison's locks. In him was prefigured what was later fulfilled in our Lord and Saviour. For just as Joseph was sent to prison through the plotting and accusation of his mistress, so Christ was crucified through the plotting and accusation of the synagogue, and deigned to descend to the underworld as if into a prison. See the likeness. Of Joseph it is written that he was free in the prison and had received authority over those held in it. And what is written of our Lord and Saviour? "They have laid me," he says, "in the lowest pit, in dark places and in the shadow of death. I have become like a man without help, free among the dead." This was fulfilled more truly in Christ, who not only had power over those bound in prison but also, from the very prison of hell, mightily and happily took back the spoil that the devil had seized. "Ascending on high, he led captivity captive"; that is, those whom the devil had taken captive to death, he took back to life.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us too, following the example of the blessed Joseph, hasten as far as we can, with God's help, to flee from dangerous and suspicious familiarity, so that we may keep the brightness of chastity, according to what the Apostle says: "Flee fornication." Against other sins we must fight; to keep chastity safe, we must flee. Let us imitate the blessed Joseph, then, in perfect love and in guarding chastity, so that we may not wish to repay even our enemies evil for evil, and so that we may deserve to keep the ornaments of purity in this world in such a way that we may be set free from eternal disgrace, by the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
B. Various Sermons.
23. TO MONKS, I.

Beloved, we have come to this place not for rest, not for security, but for battle, for combat. We have come forward here for a contest; we have come up to wage war against the vices. For our vices are our enemies, of which Scripture declares: "Take care never to make a covenant with them." We need, brothers, watchful care and tireless vigilance, because this conflict has no end and this enemy knows no peace. You can be defeated by this enemy, but you cannot take him into friendship. And so the battle we have undertaken is hard enough and dangerous enough, because it is waged within a man and does not end except with the man himself.

This is why we have betaken ourselves to this quiet retreat and spiritual camp: so that every day we may fight against our passions in unwearying combat; so that every day we may subject our wills to our elders like handmaids; so that we may cut away the wickedness of the heart and sheathe the sword of the tongue; so that we not only refrain from wronging one another but do not even feel the wrongs others inflict on us. For these things belong especially to our profession: to seek no comfort in this life, no honour; to shun the consolations of present things and prepare the mind for the promised rewards of eternal recompense; to rejoice in subjection and lowliness; to seek poverty eagerly; and to root out of our hearts not only possessions but our very wills. To have nothing of one's own is sometimes forced on us by necessity, but to desire nothing is a matter of virtue.

We should also know this: we who have resolved to live among one another are diligent or negligent either with great fruit or with great danger. Happy, then, is the soul that, by living well in the community, is a joy to many, and by which a great many are built up or enlightened. For good things increase when they are shared with many. This is what the saying of that wisest of men refers to: "My son, if you are wise, you will be wise for yourself and for your neighbours." So if someone living in the community offers an example of humility or patience to those who follow him, as much good as he lends from himself to his neighbours, so much gain from others does he turn to himself. But if, on the contrary, through disobedience or pride (which, worse still, is usually more easily found), he draws others into an example of evil or wickedness, then for as many as he has destroyed he incurs the danger of damnation, for as many as he has harmed he takes on losses, and the sin that once went out from him will flow back upon him many times over. So just as that man is greatly to be admired and praised whose good course is the progress of many, so that man is rightly to be mourned whose life is the ruin of many.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since we are placed among others, let us take care to do what builds them up, so that our life may not harm the virtues of others, our lukewarmness may not weaken their fervour, our anger may not violate their patience, our pride may not corrupt their humility, our foulness may not defile their beauty, and we may not put out the burning lamps of others if we cannot light our own. Indeed, those foolish virgins, however foolish they were, did not wish so much to put out others' lamps as to light their own. So, after their example, if any of us lacks the rich grace of humility, or the fire of faith, or the flame of fervour, or the oil of love, or the light of discernment, let him come to those he sees have more of it, and let him draw the grace into himself not by taking it from his neighbours but by imitating them, and so lay hold of the goods of another's possession not only without loss to it but even with gain. For a great fire that has been kindled never feels any loss of light, nor does the multitude of those looking at the sun diminish its light. However many look to it, to that many it lends its gifts, and yet it always remains whole.

Blessed by God is the soul whose humility puts another's pride to shame, whose patience quenches a neighbour's anger, whose obedience silently rebukes another's sloth, whose fervour rouses the sluggishness of another's lukewarmness, who by the grace of consolation and edification enlightens the eye of a neighbour's heart when it is troubled by anger. Such a one is better off than the man who, when a brother has been somewhat saddened by someone, does not stretch out his hand to lift him up with comfort, but instead, by the push of his evil talk, helps him to fall as he totters like a leaning wall; and when that brother has been corrected for his good as discipline requires, stirs him up with wicked counsel only to dash him down, arms him only to destroy him.

So, brothers, the man for whom his own evils are not enough acts in such a way as to incur judgment for the ruin of others too. Let us be certain, beloved, that unless we are on our guard, unless every day we cut back and cut away our passions, we shall become much worse than we were while we lived in the world, so that our last state becomes worse than our first. And indeed, beloved, as long as we were serving the world in those deeds and affairs of which we are now ashamed, the adversary did not oppose us; rather, he agreed with us, because in our wretched and lost life he found nothing on which to exercise his envy. Our works pleased him; our crimes and sins were enough for him by themselves. For who would make war on his own soldier, and who would want to attack his own subject? But that man's life was beyond all unhappiness whom the enemy did not even think worth harming.

But now, since we have renounced his pleasures, he has seen his worshippers return to the service of their original Maker; he has seen his idols in us changed, in a way, into the temple of God; and gnashing his teeth like a roaring lion, the ever-watchful plotter searches out every way to do harm. Of this lion the Apostle bears witness: "Be watchful, for your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour." Blessed are those whom this lion judges worth hunting and following, surely by the footprints of their virtues and the scent of their merits. For only the good are hunted by him, since the wicked offer themselves of their own accord. After the former he runs violently; the latter he runs into without even trying. Blessed, then, are those whom this lion is driven by envy to seek and is not permitted by his malice to find. It does indeed sound terrible in our ears when we hear: "like a roaring lion." But since it is said, "His food is choice," his seeking is a sign of our being chosen, and his roaring is a sign of his despair, as we read in another place: "He will gnash his teeth and waste away." The divine word speaks in such a way that consolation is joined to terror. That he gnashes his teeth belongs to a bloodthirsty foe, but that he wastes away belongs to a defeated one. And amid all this, the enemy's jealousy betrays how great are the things God has prepared for man.

So, beloved, as we think on these things and toil in this contest, let us remember that we are the disciples and the sons of our glorious and illustrious father. Let each of us seize what he can from the goods of a father who left no will. Let one take from the inheritance the silken robe of faith, the precious variety of his deeds; let another lay hold of the talent of gentleness and simplicity; let another claim for himself the adornment of a kindly heart and the necklace of wisdom; let another take possession of the pearl of compunction and the treasure of chastity.
