For although that richest friend of God took with him whole everything he had, he nevertheless left it all to us, if we are willing. Let us act, then, following his good works, so that he who will be raised to eternal glory and restored at the end of the ages may already rise again now for the Church through his merits brought back to life in his sons.
24. TO MONKS, II.

Whatever sermon I offer here, I offer because God supplies the strength and because your brotherhood, in a way, lovingly asks it of me. I do it not out of any presumption, but out of true and complete love. By God's grace you are so far advanced that you have very little need of our warning. Still, at the command of love, which knows no fear, we venture to suggest and urge, with true humility and complete love, even what we know you already do very well. We do not do it without embarrassment, though, since we know we are not yet fit even to be disciples, and here we seem to be rousing masters to holy work. Lukewarm ourselves, we are obliged to admonish the fervent; sinners, we rebuke the righteous; unskilled, we instruct the learned; and while we are still tossed by the endless waves on the sea of this world, we preach to those who have already happily reached harbour.

Yet, dearly beloved brothers, ships that have overcome and come through the waves of the open sea are often in trouble even in the safest harbour, and unless great care is taken they very nearly sink. So, with the deepest humility and great reverence, we urge you on this point. Christ has freed you from deadly sins as from dangerous waves, and you have been set in the harbour of peace and blessedness. Now, with Christ's help, keep watch and be quick to bail out continually the small negligences and, as it were, the tiny sins that seep into the soul the way drops gather in the bilge through the tiniest cracks in a ship. For a ship that has escaped the waves of the sea fills with the tiniest drops and sinks if it is not bailed out in harbour. In the same way a monk who has overcome and come through the sins of this world, as through dangerous waves, and has reached the harbour of the monastery, runs the risk of shipwreck in the harbour itself if he neglects to bail the creeping vices and small daily sins out of the bilge of his soul.

But someone says, “How can the soul be bailed out?” By praying, of course, by fasting, by keeping vigil, and by showing true love, true humility and true obedience. Listen carefully, brothers, I beg you. A ship is bailed out with a bucket, and in the same way the soul is freed from evil works by the Lord's Prayer, if a man says it and says it truthfully: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” Whoever has mercifully pardoned all who sin against him will have no trace of any sin left in his soul. Listen, brothers, and notice what I said: whoever pardons the one who sins against him. I did not say that you ought to pardon someone who has sinned against God. I said that if anyone has sinned against you, you ought to forgive him. What is worse, we are sometimes slow or reluctant to forgive someone who has sinned against us, yet quick to pardon someone who has offended God. But if we want to act justly, we must not pardon at all, without very strict discipline, someone who has sinned against God. Otherwise, while he is let off through misplaced kindness, he becomes an example of ruin to others. So let each person show himself merciful in matters that concern himself, for the Lord says: “If you forgive men their sins, your heavenly Father will forgive you your sins.”

But when someone dares to commit a sin against God, he must undergo monastic discipline. This should be done in a good and loving spirit, so that he is corrected by spiritual chastisement in this world and does not perish in the world to come, since every sin not corrected in this world will be punished in the age to come. That is what divine Scripture says about a son or a servant: “You beat him with the rod, and you will deliver his soul from hell.” And so, as I suggested above, let us beware not only of deadly sins, but let us also spit out our small negligences every day as if they were the devil's poison. For there are some who, after professing the religious life, grow slack through too much self-assurance because they seem to have left the world. In them the Lord's saying is fulfilled: “Would that you were cold or hot! But now, because you are lukewarm, I will begin to spew you out of my mouth.” What does he mean by “Would that you were hot or cold”? He means this: it would have been better for you to stay cold in the world, or to be fervent in the monastery. But now you have left the world, and through your negligence you have refused to take hold of spiritual fervour. You have become lukewarm, and you are spewed out of the Lord's mouth, hardly ever to be taken back.

Therefore, dearest brothers, with God's help pay careful attention to the saying of divine Scripture: “Keep your heart with all vigilance.” We should rejoice over a monk who is willing in the monastery to show gentleness, obedience and patience, meek and humble. In the same way we must grieve over one who seems to have left this world only in body, while in his heart he is known either to have faithlessly stayed in the world or to have unhappily gone back to it. In place of humility he displays pride, in place of patience anger, in place of obedience contempt, and in place of the medicine of love he pours out the poison of malice. To such people applies blessed Peter's true and very fearful saying: “It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back.” And again: “The dog has returned to its vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mire.” But we must not despair even of such people, brothers. When you pray, God is able to kindle a spark of compunction and to burn up all worldly pleasure, like the thorns and thistles of wickedness, with a healing fire, the very fire of which the Lord says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I want but that it be kindled?”

So pray, dearly beloved brothers, not only that God may grant you good perseverance, but also that those who are negligent may at last lift themselves out of the pit of pride and free themselves from its snares. For if, through your prayers and your loving counsel, any who are lukewarm and negligent are reformed, the Lord will repay you with a double reward, both for your own correction and for theirs. Those who are good must not exalt themselves as though by their own merits, and those who are negligent must not despair of God's mercy. Rather, let the good guard God's gifts with humility, and let the negligent, with great compunction, hurry all the faster to penance or to the remedies of correction. For the good man who begins to be proud will be humbled, and the proud man who humbles himself will be raised up by God's mercy. All that matters is that he not allow himself to be weighed down any longer by that very harsh yoke, nor be hardened any further by persisting in his sins through excessive and dangerous indifference. Let him instead flee so quickly to God's mercy that no trace of sin is left in him. A poultice or a suture is best applied while the wounds are still fresh. If the will to rise again turns quickly to the heavenly physician, no trace of sin can remain with the one who has fallen, because under the hand of God, the almighty physician, the disease swiftly vanishes and the sick man is quickly healed.

Again and again I ask and urge you, brothers, to be constantly eager to show obedience, humility and love not only to your elders and equals but also to those younger than you. For whatever good things a servant of God strives to possess, he quickly loses them all if there is no true humility and love in him. Do not grumble, brothers, for it is written that the grumblers were destroyed by serpents. Do not slander, brothers, for it is written: “Whoever slanders his brother will be rooted out.” Do not nurse anger in your heart, for it is written: “The anger of man does not work the righteousness of God.” Do not hate one another, because it is written: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer.”

But there is no need to go on teaching your holy charity with words, since we know, and rejoice, that you carry it out in deeds to the glory of Christ. We make only this special request. Since God has been pleased to place you in a place of quiet and calm, pray all the more earnestly to the Lord for us, who are battered by the storms and countless waves of this world. Then, even if glory is not given to us, because we do not deserve it, at least forgiveness of sins may be granted through your prayers. Amen.
XXV. SERMON BEFORE LENT.

I ask and urge you, dearest brothers, that in this season, established by law and most holy, no one presume to take a midday meal except on Sundays, unless perhaps someone whose illness does not allow him to fast. On other days fasting is either a remedy or a source of reward, but in Lent not fasting is a sin. Whoever fasts at another time will receive pardon; whoever is able to fast in Lent and does not will feel the penalty. Even the man who is not strong enough to fast should prepare what he is to eat at home, privately, for himself alone, or together with another sick person if there is one. He should not invite those who are healthy and able to fast to eat with him. If he does, not only God but people too can see that he is not unable to fast because of illness, but unwilling to fast because of gluttony. Let it be enough for him that he himself cannot fast, and let him eat rather with groans and sighs and grief of heart, because others are fasting and he cannot. Let every sick person have what he needs prepared privately, either for himself alone or likewise for another sick person. He must not invite a healthy person to a meal, or he will add to his own sin the sin of the other's gluttony.

Because he cannot fast, however, he ought to give more generously to the poor, so that by giving alms he may redeem the sins he cannot heal by fasting. It is good to fast, brothers, but it is better to give alms. If someone can do both, it is a double good. But if he cannot, it is better to give alms. If fasting is not possible, almsgiving is enough without fasting, but fasting without almsgiving is not enough at all. So if someone cannot fast, almsgiving without fasting is good. If he is able to fast and give alms, it is a double good. But fasting without almsgiving is no good at all, unless someone is so poor that he has nothing whatever to give. For those who have nothing to give, a good will is enough, according to what is written: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

But who will be able to excuse himself, when the Lord has promised to give a reward even for a cup of cold water? And why did he say “cold”? So that no poor man could excuse himself on the grounds that he had no firewood, or say that he had no pot to heat the water in. Moreover, dearest brothers, through the blessed prophet the Lord encourages and urges almsgiving in such a way that there is hardly a poor man who can excuse himself. For he says: “This is the fast that I have chosen, says the Lord: break your bread for the hungry.” He did not say to give a whole loaf, since that poor man might perhaps have no other. He says “break”, which is to say: even if you are so poor that you have only one loaf, still break off some of it and give it to the poor man. “And bring the needy and homeless into your house,” he says. If someone is so poor that he has nothing with which to give the poor man food, let him at least prepare a bed for a stranger in one corner of his house.

What are we to say to this, brothers, or what excuse can we have? We have large and spacious houses and scarcely ever deign to take in a stranger. We do not know, or rather do not believe, that Christ is received in every stranger, as he himself said: “I was a stranger and you took me in,” and: “As often as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me.” We find it tiresome and distasteful to receive Christ in the poor in our own country. I fear he may repay us in kind and not receive us into his blessedness. We despise him in this world; I fear he may despise us in turn in heaven, as he himself said: “For I was hungry and you gave me nothing to eat, I was a stranger and you did not take me in,” and: “As often as you did not do it to one of the least of these, you did not do it to me.” And as for what follows, brothers, may God turn it away from us, for he then added: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.”

Let us not hear these things in passing, then, dearest brothers, or with our bodily ears alone. Let us hear them faithfully, and teach others by word and example alike, so that they too may hold to them and fulfil them. What, then, did the Lord say next through the prophet? “If you see the naked,” he says, “clothe him.” In this matter I judge no one; let each look to his own conscience. But I accuse and reproach myself, because it has perhaps sometimes happened through negligence that my bits of clothing, which the poor ought to have received, were eaten by moths. And I fear that the very garments may be brought forward as witnesses against me on the day of judgement, as the apostle James terrifyingly warns: “Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that will come upon you. Your riches have rotted and your garments have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a witness against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have stored up treasure on earth and fattened your hearts in luxury on the day of slaughter.” All these threats, dearest brothers, which Christ made through the apostle, terrify us greatly, as I said. Yet we must not despair of God's mercy. For even now I and negligent people like me can, with God's help, amend ourselves if we are willing: if we give more generously the alms we have given too sparingly until now, and if, with grief and groaning and with hope of restoration, we implore God's mercy for our past sins.

So, as we suggested above, dearest brothers, let the richness of almsgiving commend our fasts, for a fast without almsgiving is like a lamp without oil. A lamp lit without oil can smoke but cannot give light. In the same way, fasting without almsgiving does torment the flesh, but it does not enlighten the soul with the light of love. For now, brothers, while we can, as regards the present season, let us fast in such a way that our midday meals are given to the poor, so that what we would have eaten we store up not in our purses but in the stomachs of the poor, for the poor man's hand is Christ's treasury. Whatever it receives is stored up in heaven so that it does not perish on earth. Though the food the poor man receives is consumed, the reward of the good deed is laid up in heaven. But if we take care to spend the cost of our midday meals on supper, with choice flavours and dish after dish, the pleasures of our body are not reduced but doubled. And just as our body loses nothing this way, so our soul gains nothing.

I give this warning, brothers, out of fear rather than because I believe anything bad of you. I know, in fact, that by God's grace many of you constantly take in strangers and often give alms to the poor. So let what I suggest serve this purpose: that whoever was doing this may do more of it, and whoever was not doing it, or was perhaps slow to do it, may make so holy a work, so pleasing to God, his habit. And I believe that, inspired by God, your charity always keeps chastity, even with your own wives, for many days before the feasts as they come round. Yet, though it may be superfluous, out of love I also remind you of what I believe you already do. With God's help, keep chastity throughout Lent until the end of Easter. Then, at that most holy Easter solemnity, clothed in the light of love, shining with almsgiving, adorned with prayers, vigils and fasts as with heavenly and spiritual pearls, and at peace not only with your friends but also with your enemies, you may approach the Lord's altar with a free and untroubled conscience and receive his body and blood not for judgement but for healing.

But while I am speaking of almsgiving, let no one in straitened poverty be troubled. Whoever has done what he could has fulfilled everything, because a complete will to do it will be counted as the deed itself. But only the one who is willing to regard every poor person as himself can fulfil this. Let him give to the poor as he would wish it done to himself if he were in such need. Whoever does this will fulfil the commandments of both the New and the Old Testament, carrying out that Gospel saying: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them. For this is the Law and the Prophets.” May the Lord himself bring us, under his protection, to this law of true and perfect love, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.
XXVI. SERMON ON LENT.

I believe you are puzzled, dearly beloved brothers, as to why we hurried ahead to the previous Sunday, and why, though Lent begins today, we began to keep its observance a week early. This early observance cannot be faulted. It is a mark of devotion to carry out the law before learning its statutes, and to obey the commandments before the commandments of obedience compel us. The one belongs to love, the other to fear; the one is required by command, the other is offered out of piety; in the one a debt is paid, in the other a gift is presented. So we too have presented a pious gift to God by fasting longer. A feast kept early cannot be faulted. In times of joy, our longings always run ahead of the solemnity, and devotion, in its eagerness, anticipates the joy to come. So this was done not only blamelessly but also prudently. In uncertain matters it is always right to add something extra for safety, because what is extra can be cut back, but what is too little cannot be lengthened. That is what happened in this observance. Because we fasted longer for Lent's sake, we have not shortened Lent; it remains whole for us. But if we had fasted less, we could not have restored it to its full number of days.

But perhaps the question is why the fast we have kept does not count toward Lent for us. It will certainly benefit us. Even if it does not count toward Lent, it counts toward salvation; if it does not add to the number, it adds to our merit. Whom has it ever failed to profit to pray, to read, to fast? Whom have chastity, sobriety and gentleness failed to profit? Except that I find more fault with those who were ready to fast but, after they heard of the solemnities, neglected to fast during the uncertain days. They surely showed that they live religiously not willingly but under compulsion. I suppose they were afraid that if the fast were lengthened by five days, their flesh and body would give out, and that, thin and frail, they would not be able to endure the abstinence of Lent.

So let all hear, the well-fed and the robust alike, the thin and the pale, that today is Lent. Let the former hear, I say, so that they may begin to fast; let the latter not stop abstaining. And let them all hurry together into Christ's ark. Indeed, let the former hurry all the more because they began abstaining later, so that they may enter more disciplined and purer, for in times of danger the Lord's ark is strong enough to carry the one who fasts, but it cannot bear the drunkard. So, as we have said before, we urge you, people of our own time, to flee eagerly, each of you, from the whirlwinds of this world to the house of God, just as righteous Noah urged the people of his time. He urged them, and never stopped preaching the flood to come. And though the voice of his preaching went unheard, still, though his tongue was silent, he spoke by his work; though he held back from speaking aloud, his axe rang out. For while he was building so great a structure, the work itself bore witness to the reason that ark was being made. By its very construction it testified that new dwellings would be needed for new dangers. Any wise man could have understood that some sort of shipwreck was threatening when such a house was being built, a house that would not cling to the ground but float on the deep, when such a lodging was being prepared, one whose floor would not be fixed to the ground and which the waves would not sink. What wise man, I say, would not have understood that the flood was at hand when he saw such a dwelling being built, one that would not so much shut in those it took in as carry them, and would not so much keep off showers of rain as ward off the storms of shipwreck? What people, I say, would not have been warned of danger by a lodging in which one was not to live, but rather to be an exile? That they would be wanderers in whatever part of the world, dwelling and all: this is what holy Noah preached to the peoples by his work, and he was speaking that saying of the Lord in the Gospel: “If you do not believe me, believe the works.”
XXVII. SERMON ON THE FEAST OF THE DEPOSITION OF ST AUGUSTINE.

Today, dearest brothers, we celebrate the burial of our lord and father Augustine the bishop, of holy memory. As I silently marvel within myself at his apostolic merits, I am reminded of the dress and vestments of that high priest Aaron, which prefigured various graces and virtues. Under the ordinances of the Old Testament, according to the venerable mysteries of the ancient law, the great high priest was adorned with various insignia when he was about to enter the Holy of Holies. These beautiful and varied things showed wonders to those who saw them and sacraments to those who understood them. Among them was a row of bells, skilfully fastened along the hems of the tunic that flowed down to his feet and around its lowest edge at his feet, and they rang all about his venerable step, so that the vesture itself showed that the high priest was not allowed to be silent in the holy place. And when the priest entered the Holy of Holies, the bells rang out not in any other place but at the very edges of his garments. Without doubt this signified that whenever a priest enters the temple of God he must not cease to cry out about the last things of this world and the end of the age, always proclaiming the rewards of the just and the punishments of sinners. Then, while the one group is spurred on to good and the other is deterred from evil, they may come together to eternal rewards. Hence I too am not now afraid of being presumptuous in preaching confidently about so great a patron, our own Saint Augustine. He was spiritually clothed and endowed with the dowry of such great virtues. I do not fear, I say, that it is presumption if I profess myself to be, as it were, one bell on the hem of his garment. Clinging, as it were, about the footsteps of his teaching, I may receive the sound of my voice from his merits. Set in motion by his virtues as if by his movements, I may give back some ringing, however slight, and strike your hearts by recalling his merits.

Besides these ornaments, which, as we have recalled, divine kindness granted to Saint Augustine in the light of his merits, we read of yet another likeness in the Old Testament. On the high priest's forehead a plate of gold was stretched across and shone brightly, so that the gleam of the metal would display purity of conscience. A jewelled shoulder-piece was also fitted to him, and a precious ornament on his breast, so that the dignity of the outer man might remind him how the inner man was to be cultivated. On that breast-ornament Aaron the priest also bore the names of the sons of Israel, worked into it by the jeweller's craft. We rejoice that this magnificence, like those sacred vestments of his, shines in the praiseworthy teachings of the lord Augustine of holy memory and in the spiritual pearls of various graces. Indeed, in him these things are shown to have shone far more fully and far more truly. They were represented as images in Aaron's vestments, but in Augustine they are plainly expressed, whether in his grace or in his merits. In the one, a plate of gold adorned the brow. In the other, golden modesty and precious sincerity light up the brow of the mind. Those ancient ornaments of foreign stone and insignia of elaborate beauty were seen to be put on Aaron, but they are shown to have been granted to Augustine by the bounty of grace. In Aaron they were sketched in outline by a craftsman's hand; in Saint Augustine they were perfected by the gift of the Creator. Aaron put them on once a year, only to take them off again soon. Augustine knows how to put them on as part of his very nature and does not know how to take them off. They are never to be laid aside, not even with the body, but are to be carried back with the spirit to their author. In the one was a passing figure; in the other, an abiding truth.

It remains for you to make progress in all things through the heavenly teachings and singular examples of Saint Augustine. Everything is abundantly at hand for you in him: what pertains to edification, what looks toward glory, what calls to life, and what raises up to glory. If you look in him for the disposition of good will, his works of mercy cry out. If you desire patience, the ornaments of gentleness appear. If the secrets of a pure conscience are to be questioned, the marks of chastity answer. The balsams of kindness and the spices of piety give off their fragrance, and the jewels of knowledge and wisdom shine. Amid all this we greatly fear that the poverty of our speech may hide the merits of Saint Augustine even as affection prompts us to proclaim them. Before this follower of heavenly things put off secular dress and took up the standards of sacred service, he served for some time in secret as a hidden soldier, in fear and awe of the Lord. Though long placed in this world, he stood at the world's edge. And so, when he took up a public religious life, he did not so much begin to be what he was not as reveal what had lain hidden. In his youth the deceits of wantonness prevailed, and the fleeting sweetness of passing and ruinous pleasures tried to paint images of transient things on his senses and impress them there. The world bound him with various ties and added violent force. He was strong in birth, means, character, sharpness of mind and a capacious memory, and through his riches he brought the gifts of manifold grace into public view, so the pleasantness of this life sought in a way to hold him in its embrace. Yet he felt that all these delights were so many chains about him. He resolved to refuse his trust to uncertain things and determined that he could not consent to them. In slippery evils, things are thought pleasant precisely because they pass quickly, as if after showing their bloom. To him, for that very reason, they were all the more suspect: they capture their follower by their appearance, ruin him with pleasure, and desert him by their swiftness.

So he considered all the empty things of the present age and gathered them before his eyes. He looked down on them as from the citadel of wisdom and rejected them as nothing compared with eternal things. Then, within himself and in his faith, he armed his heart, already filled with God, with the encouragements and conversations of his will: "From now on I plainly have nothing in common with you, passing form of a deceitful world. In this one way I shall win the victory: by abandoning you. I shall not incur loss again through using you; rather, I shall win a shining palm over you. How nothing you are, vanity of earthly things, and yet at times how much! You command much while you are held, but you bestow more when you are rejected. When you are desired, you take your followers captive. When you are despised, you glorify those who despise you, and through hatred of you and flight from you you will confer great riches." What more need be said? Saint Augustine was shut in amid the shipwrecks of this life and set in the midst of the waves of the world. He was placed, as it were with Jonah, in the jaws of that devouring and monstrous beast, and he cried to the Lord from the depths. Then the world, though unwilling, vomited him out and sent him forth for the advancement of all the churches, for whose benefit he was being prepared. It is the nature of righteousness and virtue that the more eagerly and the longer it wishes to be hidden, the more clearly it becomes known, and the very hiding betrays it. So his fame, aware of such great goods, flew everywhere among the peoples and shone far and wide with the fragrance of a most delightful sweetness. Even in a lowly place he stood out, to the admiration of all, like a city set on the top of a mountain. The lamp could no longer lie hidden under the bushel, nor could its overflowing greatness, a light [?] like a star, be received or contained within its hiding place. So a great lamp is not lit for itself. It casts its light far off and all around, pouring out a beautiful light with the flaming brilliance of doctrine, and it was present whole to all and entire to each. This is the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through endless ages of ages. Amen.
28. SERMON ON THE REVELATION OF THE BODY OF BLESSED STEPHEN, TO BE READ ON THE FEAST OF ITS FINDING.

In the present reading we have heard of a vision celebrated in all the churches. We have heard not of dreams mocked by the slippery error of the senses, but of oracles proven by their results. We are right to believe the revelation as it is told, since we hold its fruit as a gift. Where are those who say that pious honours should not be paid to the martyrs? Look: this man has long enjoyed the blessed splendour of paradise, and he is now shown to the world for this very purpose, that he may be venerated. Hence God, who dispenses what benefits us, plainly commands that the one he allowed to be found should be honoured.

The account of the revelation says, then, that neither bird nor beast violated that sacred body. Where are those who want the sacred ashes of the martyrs to appear unhonoured? Look: the brute nature of beasts and birds has no understanding, yet it renders diligent service to a friend and shuns an unlawful touch, revering perhaps the secret of an angelic guard. No bird touched him, no beast violated him. The reverence of the beasts already condemns man and casts great reproach on his cruelty. The more the impiety of a hardened heart [?] … the savagery of beasts passes over to us, and our humanity passes to the beasts. This man was the first minister and the first martyr of the newborn Church. Carried up by the ardour of glory, he rose to the very summit and pinnacle of merit, and the Levite of Christ's altar suddenly became the priest of his own blood. After that singular and glorious victory of the Lord, he led a contest no one had yet fought, brought about a new triumph, and bore the standard of the white-robed army; he offered himself to God as the devoted firstfruits of martyrdom. He was a herald of the truth and a follower of the Redeemer. The impious Jewish people, still hot from their recent parricide, were panting after the crime of a monstrous outrage, and by them he was slain under a hard shower of stones. He was made more beautiful by his many wounds, and whiter by his blood-stained garment. To this end he had been prepared by various graces from his earliest years and by the teachings of the Law and the Prophets.

Blessed is he whose life was happily lived and more happily spent. Blessed is he whose life was set forth as an example to the world, completed in witness to God, and taken up into the patronage of the whole world. Blessed is he in whom an illustrious life trampled on death; or rather, in whom death was the price paid for life. Others are consumed under the penalty of the ancient transgression, by a common lot and a general end, or by fevers and the various kinds of mortality laid upon us. Blessed is this man. He poured out his spotless spirit for the honour of Christ and so turned nature's necessity into an occasion of glory. He earned the right to turn the debt owed by his condition into the gain of virtue. What the law of origin and of guilt had claimed for itself in man since ages past, devotion claimed entirely for praise in him. And so, after the Lord's triumph, cruel death learned for the first time in him that it could be conquered even by a servant. It grew accustomed to bring forth life from itself for the martyrs who would follow, though [?] in life. The gates of righteousness were opened, and he toiled in spiritual contests with heaven as his witness. Filled with the Holy Spirit and with a mind made drunk by God, he spoke out thus: "Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God." Full of the Spirit, then, and seeing the Son of Man at the right hand, he carried out the offices of his passion under the gaze of the Trinity. So the divine word testifies about him and about the Jews: "They saw his face," it says, "as the face of an angel." Surely the brightness of his mind had poured itself wholly even into outward beauty. With such a countenance [?] the presence of an angel, he who had seen the face of God. So the Jews saw his face as the face of an angel. It is a large share of damnation when the wicked are not allowed to remain unaware of their crime. They saw his face as the countenance of an angel, so that they could not gain the fruit of their hatred, but [?] for their admonition. Even in the present moment they beheld the glory of the man they were persecuting, so that they almost received a share of it through their eyes. They understood that the man whose destruction through their fury they rejoiced at was being consecrated through their own agency: they saw his face. If he appeared like this in battle, how do we think he will appear in the kingdom? And God, the judge of merits, who adorned him with such beauty as he died, with what do you think he will clothe him when he rises? Then, kneeling down, he prayed, saying: "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." As he died, he gladly pleaded for those who caused his death, because the glory of a precious death was not hidden from him. "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." Do you think that he will ever stop interceding for those who pray to him, when he prayed for his persecutors? If he repaid stones like this, what will he give in return for prayers? If he interceded while being stoned, what will he do when he is called upon?

It was not nobility or wealth that made this man a son and an angel of God, but faith: he believed in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. He signed this confession of God not with his hand, nor with his lips alone, but with his blood, and he swore to it by his death.

But you say: "No authority of Scripture says that honour should be paid to the martyrs." Then what of the prophet's declaration through the Holy Spirit: "But to me your friends are greatly to be honoured, O God"? He could show them no greater honour than to proclaim them friends of God and to believe that in their persons he was honouring God. "But to me your friends are greatly to be honoured, O God" means this: "I embrace your benefits, Lord, in the merits of your servants. I marvel at your gifts in their virtues. And in your servants, because of your gifts, I rightly venerate you." Our God testifies that he is clothed in the one who is cold, fed in the hungry and honoured in the poor, saying: "Whoever did it to one of these least ones did it to me." It follows that we must believe he speaks and thinks this way about his elect: "The reverence that anyone strives to pay to my saints, he pays to me. It is fitting that one who honoured me in his blood should be honoured in my name." Divine providence, then, has appointed these physicians for human weaknesses, so that in a mutual and joyful exchange the intercessor [?] by his worshipper, and the worshipper by his intercessor. Since this is so, dearly beloved, let us venerate the sacred and venerable ashes of the martyrs with all the strength we have. Then, by their prayers, we may obtain the pardon for our sins that we cannot obtain by our own merits. This is the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives for ages of ages. Amen.
29. SERMON ON PENTECOST.

Today, dearest brothers, everything that has been read to us fits the feast. The psalm says: "Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit." The Gospel says: "The Spirit of truth is coming." And the book of the Acts of the Apostles says: "They were all filled with the Holy Spirit." So everything has been fulfilled and completed. The psalm asked for the coming of the Holy Spirit, the Gospel promised that he would come, and the book of the Acts of the Apostles recorded that he had already come. Nothing in the order of divine things is missing from these readings: in the prophet there is petition, in the Gospel promise, in the Acts fulfilment. The blessed apostle Paul also bears witness about this Holy Spirit, saying: "To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another faith in the same Spirit. All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each as he wills."

But at this point someone may say: "If the Spirit distributes his gifts only to those he wills, then the one who does not receive a gift is not to blame, since the distribution of graces depends not on the wish of the one who receives but on the choice of the one who distributes." That is true, beloved. But it is true only if we understand it of miraculous powers and not of how we live. We cannot all obtain powers, even if we want them, but we can all lay hold of life if we seek it, as it is written: "For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds." The distribution of lofty and excellent graces belongs to the choice and dispensation of the Holy Spirit. Living a good life belongs to a person's faith and labour. "For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds." Let a person only ask and seek with the whole heart. The one who commanded you to seek will without doubt enable you to find. Does the divine word lie? "Knock," it says, "and it will be opened to you." Why did he command us to knock, if not because he wants to open to those who knock? Even among human beings there is no such unfairness as for someone to want to be asked who does not want to grant the request. Anyone who has no wish to give avoids the request of the one who asks. No one wants to be asked unless he has already decided within himself to give. So God, who wants to give to all, wants to be asked by all, saying: "Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find."

But perhaps someone may say: "If everyone who asks receives, then if we ask for miraculous powers we shall receive them too. Why should we not ask for powers as well, if we can receive everything we ask for?" It is not so, beloved. It is proud, and beyond the human condition, to ask for the grace of such powers. Human prayer ought to be humble, not presumptuous; it should ask only for salvation, not for vanity. No one can be without sin. What impudence it is, then, for someone to ask for powers when he cannot yet be fully sure even of pardon! It is enough, then, for a person to earn the Lord's mercy. Whoever manages to obtain forgiveness should believe that he has received from God the greatest grace of all. Whoever asks for something presumptuously deserves to receive it less for that very reason, if he presumes to ask for higher things. Moreover, a person who asks for the grace of powers may not offend God by the presumption of his prayer, yet he may still be endangered by vanity. It is not good for everyone to possess the grace of exercising powers. Those who are set in humility are better off than those puffed up with boasting of their holiness. For some, the very loftiness of these graces is dangerous. Whoever is set on a height and does not know how to stand firm falls all the harder for having climbed so high. That is why the blessed apostle says: "There are distributions of graces," and: "All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each as he wills." He rightly says "as he wills," because nothing is better for a person than what the Spirit wills. The will of the Holy Spirit knows well how to dispense his gifts. Nothing is more beneficial than for a person to have only those powers which the Holy Spirit has judged that he ought to confer on him.

Of course, if anyone wants to obtain the grace of virtues, there are virtues he may seek without blame. Let him seek chastity, take hold of sobriety, keep discipline, and love charity. With God's grace we all can and ought to have these virtues. We must not think that virtues consist only in driving out demons, curing illnesses and giving health. Every good work is a virtue. If you act well every day, if you live holily and justly, you perform holy works of virtue every day. If someone cannot drive a demon out of another person, let him at least drive out of himself the vices that come from demonic attack. If someone cannot cure the disease of another's body, let him cure the disease of his own soul. No one is required to bestow a grace of healing that God has not given him. He can achieve nothing greater than to earn his own healing.

After the labour of the vigils, a longer sermon should not tire you any further. So whoever is spiritual and wishes to hear a fuller sermon on the divinity of the Holy Spirit, let him come to church early tomorrow, eagerly and faithfully. Whoever neglects to come will show quite plainly that he is not spiritual. But we trust in God's mercy that the grace of the Holy Spirit will prevail with you over the business of this world. This is the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ages of ages. Amen.
30. SERMON ON THE HOLY TRINITY.

When the subject is God, dearest brothers, a wish to contradict does great harm, but a careful desire to ask questions does good. In the one case the mind is blocked by obstinacy; in the other the understanding is fed by inquiry. There, unbelief resists and delights in being led astray; here, obedient humility earns the right to be taught. So you, dearest brothers, prepare the vessel of your holy hearts for the divine water that flows into them, and receive in silence and quiet what we wish to set before you about the mystery of the Holy Trinity and the divinity of the Holy Spirit. From the testimony of the holy Scriptures we want to prove how the Holy Spirit can be plainly recognized as coequal with the Father and the Son in every power.

We read in the Old Testament: "In the beginning God made heaven and earth, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters." In "God" understand the Father; in "the beginning" take the Son; in the one poured out over the waters recognize the Holy Spirit. So the majesty of the one who rules was borne over the waters, already then, I believe, prefiguring the gifts of baptism. In the making of man, too, the threefold repetition of the name of God shows that this is the work not of one person but of three. For we read: "And God said, Let us make man in our image and likeness." Notice a statement that is singular in its opening and plural in what is spoken. "And God said, Let us make man." What does this mean, except that the one substance speaks and the power of the Trinity acts? See how the name of God is spoken three times in the creation of man. For we have in Genesis: "And God said, Let us make man"; and again, "God created man"; and a third time, "God blessed him." God said, God made, God blessed: the Father said, the Son made, the Holy Spirit blessed. Because there are three persons, the one divinity is named three times. In this passage understand clearly the mystery of the unity as well. See, the image and likeness of God is given to each human being by three, and yet it is known to be one. "God said, Let us make." Pay careful attention: one speaks, and not one acts. And again, he mixes plural with singular. He does not say "in our images and likenesses," nor indeed "in my image and likeness." So he commends the unity by the singular and the Trinity by the plural. In saying "Let us make" and "our," he sets out the number of the persons; in saying in the singular "in the image and likeness," he gathers the undivided Godhead into one substance.

When God appeared to Abraham at the door of his tent, and out of one, three wondrously presented themselves to his eyes, Abraham, aware of the majesty, worshiped one in three. In the Psalms, too, the unity is plainly marked out together with its persons: "Do not cast me away," he says, "from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me." See, the prophet, praying to the Father, dreads offending the Holy Spirit no less than the Father and the Son. "Do not cast me away," he says, "from your face." The Son is understood to be the face of the Father, just as he is the Father's image. That is why we read: "Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father also"; and again: "Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?" Mark this, unbeliever: here is the mystery of the Trinity in a complete confession. The prophet speaks to the Father, professes that the Son is the Father's face, and also testifies that the Holy Spirit is spread through all things. Of the Son, too, the Lord says to Moses: "My face will go before you." This name, "face," belongs both to the oneness of substance and to the co-eternity of majesty. Isaiah, too, counts the Holy Spirit as one within the glory of the Trinity when he says: "I saw the Lord sitting on a high throne, and the seraphim stood and cried one to another: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts." And afterward he says: "And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Go and say to this people: Hearing you will hear and not understand, and seeing you will see and not see."

Let us at least believe Paul, that most renowned herald of the truth, when he says that the Holy Spirit was that Lord of hosts whom Isaiah saw and who spoke through Isaiah. But since the passage rings with a threefold repetition, "Holy, holy, holy," let us consider whether this honor does not refer to the whole Trinity. When Isaiah says, "I saw the Lord of hosts," he is understood to be proclaiming the Father to the Jews. The evangelist John is shown to refer it openly to the Son when he says: "They could not believe in Jesus because Isaiah said: He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart. Isaiah said this when he saw the glory of the Son of God and spoke of him." And when the same Isaiah says, "And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Go and say to this people: Hearing you will hear and not understand, and seeing you will see and not see," the apostle Paul, as we have said, confirms that this Lord is the Holy Spirit. So you see that the cry "Holy, holy, holy" celebrates the whole Trinity together. And just as there is no unlikeness and no difference among these three words, so there can be no distance in the power of the Trinity.

But you say: "It is plain that the Holy Spirit is lesser, because he is called the finger of God." That is not so. When you hear it said of the Holy Spirit, "If I cast out demons by the finger of God," understand that this shows not a lessening of glory but a unity of substance, not a disparity of honor but a harmony of work. What then? Because the Holy Spirit is sometimes called the finger of God, is he therefore believed to be less than the Son and the Father? Flee from the error of this notion. Consider whether this term "finger" does not sometimes include both the Father and the Son. Let us remember that it is not one finger that is spoken of when we read: "For I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers." But you say that by "fingers" only the Son and the Holy Spirit are meant here, as a pair. So that you do not try to claim this of two persons, Isaiah in another place speaks of the Trinity by the number of three fingers only, saying: "Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers?" What could be plainer about the unity of the Trinity, what clearer? Has he not here, in three fingers, weighed the equality of a single power as on the scales of a mystery? So, as has been said, now that you have been taught about their partnership in work, do not doubt the equality of their power. In saying "Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers?" he wished to speak specifically of their shared working of power and of the unity of substance, which is shown to be one and the same in the three fingers. Although the Holy Spirit always kindles your hearts to hear the word of God, so that your holy desires can scarcely be satisfied, care must still be taken to measure out the preaching of God's word so that you may go on longing for it and it may always grow in you. So let what has been said be enough for your charity for now. And since we thought something of this sermon should be kept back for you, if you gather a little earlier tomorrow, as is your custom, then once matins are finished you will hear, without any weariness, what has been deliberately kept back, by the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor for ever and ever. Amen.
XXXI. SERMON ON THE HOLY SPIRIT
What we kept back yesterday for your charity about the divinity of the Holy Spirit you may now, if you please, hear at a fitting time and in a fitting way, in silence and quiet.

We show that the Holy Spirit has his own person; we confess the Father as unbegotten and acknowledge the Son as only-begotten. So you ask me whether the Holy Spirit must be confessed as unbegotten, or begotten, or something else. The holy Scriptures speak of the power and godhead of the Holy Spirit; whether he ought to be called begotten or unbegotten, they do not say. See what darkness unbelief makes for itself! You do not want to know what God did not want to be unknown, and you want to know what he did not command to be inquired into. Scripture did not call him begotten, so that you would not believe him to be the Son; it did not call him unbegotten, so that you would not think him the Father. Instead, to mark the distinction of his being, it testified that he proceeds from the Father, as we read: "The Paraclete, who proceeds from the Father." Since this is so, recognize at least by this that the Holy Spirit has his own person. The difference of name proves that there is a third besides the two; the unity of majesty shows that he who proceeds from God is not third in order or rank. For he who comes forth from the inmost being of God is shown to be not a creature of God but the substance of God. Do not probe how he is God when it is clear that he is God. Here the reason is hidden; the truth is not. Why ask how he is the companion and equal of the king, when it is established that he is of royal honor and royal birth? Inquiry about the name is pointless where there is no doubt about his exalted rank. And because the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, Scripture says: "Whoever does not have the Spirit of the Lord does not belong to him"; and in another place: "He breathed on them and said, Receive the Holy Spirit."

You ask whether he is unbegotten or begotten. The sacred writings have said nothing about this, and it is wrong to break into the silences of God. What God did not think fit to reveal in his Scriptures, he did not want to be asked about or known through idle curiosity. Does the glory or substance of the Holy Spirit depend on whether he is shown to be unbegotten or begotten? It takes nothing from the Son that we do not read that he is unbegotten, nor from the Father that he is not held to be begotten. In terms like these there is a distinction of name, not a difference of power or majesty. "Begotten" and "unbegotten" mark a difference of person, not of nature.

Concerning the Holy Spirit, our Lord and Savior, as he was about to go to heaven, spoke thus to his apostles: "When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send you, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me"; and again: "He will teach you all things." What does this mean, dearly beloved, that the Savior said he would send the Holy Spirit to teach the disciples? Had he not taught his apostles, or must we think that Christ's teaching was only half complete? No, without doubt. But since your faith is in the Father and in the Son and in the Holy Spirit, the Savior wished to show, by sending the Holy Spirit, that the will of God the Father would build up his churches, the passion of the Son would redeem them, and the teaching of the Holy Spirit would strengthen them. How can this be seen more clearly? How, except that God the Father sent his Son for our redemption, the Son saved us by his passion, and the Holy Spirit breathed faith into us? Thus the salvation of the churches is the work of the whole divine Trinity. For the Father in his love did not want the human race to perish, the Son freed us from destruction, and the Holy Spirit leads us to the kingdom of heaven.

Yet believe in the Holy Spirit in such a way that you think him neither the Father nor the Son, but the Spirit of the Father and the Son. This whole Trinity is one God. In it there is no unlikeness and no division. For if the spirit that is in a human being is the greater part of that human being, how can the Spirit of God be believed to be lesser? So the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but the Spirit of the Father and the Son.

That the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father, our Lord and Savior said: "The Spirit," he says, "who proceeds from the Father." That the same Holy Spirit is also the Spirit of the Son, the Apostle teaches when he says: "If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him." That is why the Lord, too, after his resurrection, says to his disciples in the Gospel: "Go and baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." "In the name," he says, not "in the names." So the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God: not three gods, but one God. Person distinguishes the three; divinity joins them. The Trinity knows nothing of greater or lesser; the Godhead is ignorant of it, for one who is God cannot fail to be perfect. Therefore, whoever does not believe in the name of the Holy Spirit gains nothing by confessing the Father and the Son.

So the Holy Spirit is to be believed with the same faith and revered with equal awe. When you say "Father, Son and Holy Spirit," you have set out the persons; when you say "God," you have shown the substance. We say Father and Son and Holy Spirit so that you do not suppose you ought to believe in one person. Likewise we say one God so that you do not think there are three natures. In these three persons, then, there can be number, but there cannot be rank. For though the Trinity admits of distinction, its equality knows no grades. In the Trinity there is nothing lesser or greater, for if anything in God is called lesser, the divinity is accused of being imperfect. Indeed, whoever says that the Holy Spirit is less in godhead than the Father or the Son wrongs not only the one he judges lesser but also the one he thinks greater. Since the whole Trinity has one equality and majesty, any insult spoken against the person of one is felt equally by the whole Trinity.

But we, beloved, who have been found worthy to be the temple of the Holy Spirit, let us, with the help of that same Holy Spirit, prepare a house into which he will delight to come and in which he will delight to dwell. Let the brightness of a pure heart invite him; let chaste modesty, like blushing roses, entice him; let undefiled virginity, like gleaming lilies in fragrance and color, entice him; let kindly charity welcome him, and generous humanity, lofty humility, cheerful mercy and pure simplicity. Let the eternal dweller, the giver of eternity, find there nothing of the old man's filth, nothing of the weaknesses that lead to falling. Let there depart the excess of the foulest pleasure, the pallor of a guilty conscience, gloomy fear, staggering drunkenness, and lust, uglier than any horror. Then, when these are gone from us, the brightness of purity will go before and open a place for the virtues, and will enclose the Holy Spirit in the dwelling prepared for him. We have urged this, beloved, so that with God's help we may labor with all our strength, as far as we can, that there be in us no avarice to offend him, no unbelief to grow sluggish, no lust to defile us, but that, thoroughly amended and pure, we may be worthy to become a dwelling place of God. And may the Holy Spirit, who we read came down upon the apostles today, deign always to dwell in us, to whom be honor and glory with the Father and the Son for ever and ever. Amen.

II. The treatise of Faustus edited by P. Pithou (Veterum aliquot Galliae theologorum scripta [Paris, 1586], pp. 124 ff.: Fausti Regii Galliae episcopi de ratione fidei ad obiecta quaedam responsio).
III. The treatise of "Faustinus" on the Creed, first edited by Caspari (Alte und neue Quellen zur Geschichte des Taufsymbols [Christiania, 1879], pp. 250 ff.).
